title: An Overview of Molecular Cell Biology- adapted for young in biology
fields: Life Sciences (Brain Sciences: Systems, Computational and Cognitive Neuroscience Track)
Life Sciences (Computational and Systems Biology Track)
syllabus:
An Overview of Molecular Cell Biology- adapted for young in biology  (course code20273051)
Dan Michael
Part 1-3: Introduction
Basic chemistry of macromolecules. The study of proteins: From the primary to the quarterly structure of proteins. X-ray crystallography, Cryo-EM, AlphaFold. The dynamic nature of proteins structure. Many proteins are enzymes but certain RNAs can be enzymes as well. The role of ionization in structure function of proteins. The role of covalent modifications. Ligands and ligand-gated channels, quarterly-enforced structures. Antibodies, from origin to physiological roles. Antibodies as tools to study molecular cell biology. Indirect immunocytochemistry. Cellular mechanisms underlying heredity: The hallmarks and complexity of life. Cell to cell inheritance of traits. From cells to organs to organisms. Evolution of species. Trans-generational heredity. Chromosome theory and chromosomes, nucleosomes. Heredity through cell division: ploidity, mitosis. Hereditary through sexual reproduction: meiosis.
Part 4: Establishing the central dogma in molecular biology
Historical millstones in genetics research: Genes, genotype-phenotype relationships, different genetic inheritance patterns and allelic configurations. From biochemical millstones in macromolecules research to the experiment by Avery, McLeod and McCarthy. Deciphering the structure of DNA. DNA replication: from building blocks to semi-conservative mode of replication. The multitude DNA repair machineries. Definition of transcription. From nucleotides to the genetic code. Translation: the ribosome, the tRNAs, aminoacyl-tRNA synthases. The ribosome as a polymerase, the translation cycle at the A, P and E sites of the ribosome. Genetics disorders stemming from defects in translation. The energy requirements during translation and proof-reading during translation.
Part 5: Regulation of gene expression
From chromosomes to chromatin organization. Histones, nucleosomes. From nucleosomes to chromosome territories. From traits (sickle cell anemia) to a gene and its alleles. Regulation of transcription. Transcription factors and their binding sites. Promotors, enhancers, the pre-initiation complex (PIC). The mediator. The role of histone modifications. Rate limiting steps in the transcriptional cycle. RNA processing: Capping, splicing and polyadenylation. Regulation of translation. Heterogeneous ribosomes. Post translation modifications.
Part 6: Recombinant DNA and reverse genetics
The restriction phenomenon between bacteria and bacteriophages. DNA cloning in plasmids and bacteriophages. Modern biotechnology: human insulin produced in bacteria. Other transgenic organisms. DNA libraries. Basic properties of cancer cells and cloning an oncogene using DNA libraries. cDNA and DNA sequencing by the Sanger method. Open reading frames. Sequence comparisons lead to functional insights. Reverse genetics. Over expression of a gene product and its implications. Immunoprecipitation. Western analysis. Expression vectors. Transfection. Viral vectors. Conditional expression. Knock out of gene expression. The polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Using PCR to generate expression vectors. PCR in forensic medicine. Reporter plasmids. Analysis of transcription factor binding sites.
Part 7: Genomes, epigenomes, transcriptomes, proteomes and interactomes
The human genome in numbers. Genome sequencing enabled by deep sequencing (sequencing by synthesis). Using deep sequencing can identify cancer causing mutations. Sequence comparisons. Comparisons and the evolution of genomes. Gene duplications enables genetic novelty. Paralogs and orthologues. Phylogenetic trees. Functional annotation. The human ENCODE project. Mutations in the DNA that control gene expression. Sequencing hundreds of thousands of human genomes: the variation between genomes (“The Variome”). Epigenetics and epigenomes: The effect of chromatin structure on the contribution of the DNA to gene expression. Cell to cell epigenetic inheritance. Transcriptomes can be determined by high-throughput methods such as RNA-seq. The non-coding genome. Regulation of gene expression by non-coding RNA (ncRNA). Inhibitor RNA (RNAi). Micro-RNA biology. Single cell RNA analysis. Specialized cell types and cells under defined physiological conditions have defined transcriptomes. The entire collection of proteins (the proteome). Protein mass spectrometry. The ubiquitin system can modify proteins. The proteasome is a major a cellular protein degradation system that shapes the proteome. Proteins and their variants can be studied biochemically to appreciate the many steps from genomes to proteomes and interactomes. The generation of functional diversity: From the genome, transcriptomes, proteomes, interactomes to phenotypes.
Part 8: Cells and their organelles under homeostasis and disease
A prototypic animal cell and a prototypic neuron. Biochemical fractionation, protein mass-spectrometry and immunohistochemistry to study sub-cellular proteomes, cell structure and function. The plasma membrane.  The major lipid in a membrane bi-layer vary. Membranal proteins: single-pass and multi-pass. The neuronal membrane. Membranes are connected to the cytoskeleton. Function and dynamics of the cytoskeleton: Actin, myosin and microtubules. Intermediate filaments, cell polarity and coordination of the cytoskeleton. Cell junctions and the extracellular matrix. The nucleus and its membrane (the nuclear envelope). The other organelles in homeostasis and stress. The mitochondria allow energy conservation and metabolic compartmentation. Mitochondrial stress. Proteins move between organelles. Intracellular organization and protein sorting. The secretory pathway begins at the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). Translation on the ER and translocation of nascent proteins into the ER. The Golgi apparatus. Secretory vesicles. ER stress and pro-inflammatory responses. The lysosome and autophagy under homeostasis and stress. The general pathway for protein sorting. The secretory pathway. The cytoskeleton: actin, microtubules, integrins and more. The basal membrane, connective tissues and cell to cell junctions. Cellular and molecular biology of neural cells. Neuronal conductivity and connectivity. Synapses. Non-invasive study of neuronal circuits by recombinant DNA methods. GCaMP.
Part 9: CRISPR-derived tools for genome editing
The milestones leading to the maturation of the new era in genome editing. The cellular DNA repair machineries which are engaged following Cas-induced DNA cut: NHEJ, HDR, MMR. Knock-out and knock-in application in basic research and gene therapy. Base editing and prime editing as the new wave of approaches.
Part 10: Cell signaling and molecular networks
Principles of cell signaling. Extracellular signaling molecules and their receptors. Endocrine, paracrine and autocrine signaling systems. Signals activate short or long intracellular pathways.  Specificity, robustness and amplification of signals. Signaling through G-Protein-coupled receptors. Some G proteins regulate the production of Cyclic AMP. The adrenaline-ignited pathway that orchestrates the flight of fight response. Receptor tyrosine kinases ignite intracellular signaling. The Ras-Raf-MAPK pathway. The signaling generated by ER stress. Down-regulation of cellular signaling. Cellular networks.  Signal transduction generated in neurons by optogenetics. Signaling in the immune system, CAR-T cells.
Part 11: Development and stem cell
An overview of embryonal development. From the blastula to cell fates. cell proliferation and the cell cycle.  From mitogens to cyclines and CDKs. Cell differentiation. Molecular genetic mechanisms that create and maintain specialized cell types. Combinatorial gene control creates many different cell types. Combination of master transcription regulators specify cell types by controlling expression of many genes. Stable patterns of gene expression can be transmitted to daughter cells. The developmental potential of cells. Spatial patterning. Cell memory and complex tissue patterns. Lateral inhibition can generate complex tissue patterns. Developmental biology provides insights into disease and tissue maintenance. Morphogenesis and growth. The proliferation, death and size of cells determine organ and organism size. Hormones coordinate growth through the body. The dynamics of gene expression in embryogenesis at a single cell resolution. Methods and applications for single cell and spatial multi-omics. Stem cells and tissue homeostasis. Stem cells self-renew and produce differentiated cells. Self-renewal in the intestine and the body surface. Stem cell niche. Tissue aging.
Part 12: Modern forward genetics
Classical forward genetics. miR-assisted forward genetics. Forwards genetics necessitates a follow up by reverse genetics approaches. CRISPR-KO assisted reverse genetics. CRISPR-dCas9-activator-assisted reverse genetics. Four primary research papers will be discussed in detail.
Part 13: Hypothesis-driven research and methodologies-based expansion of knowledge
Participants in the course are expected to be raising descriptive-associated or hypothesis-associated questions referring to topics taught in the course, thus conceptually extending any given research approach/results. This part should enable students to theoretically apply the different methodologies taught in the course. This will be done throughout earlier parts of the course as well.
learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course, students aim to:
• Discuss the chemistry and dynamics of cellular macromolecules as well as the modules defined in the central dogma of molecular biology.
• Discuss the regulation of gene expression, recombinant DNA in research and biotechnology, genomes, genome editing, epigenomes, transcriptomes, proteomes, and interactomes.
• Discuss cells and their organelles in homeostasis and disease, cell signaling, developmental biology, and frontiers in functional biology.
• Appreciate an inventor’s mind that led to the emergence of a research breakthrough, often recognized by receiving a Nobel Prize, as well as the research methodologies used, and differentiate between methodologies that promote forward and reverse genetics.
• Acquire the ability to raise hypotheses based on prior scientific knowledge in molecular cell biology.
• Acquire skills to design experiments in molecular biology in order to address a hypothesis of interest, thus better understanding the process involved in generating relevant hypothesis-driven molecular data.
• Interpret the data in recently published selective articles in molecular cell biology as well as critically interpret the data using original ideas to corroborate the research findings.
• Given the student’s own discipline of origin, define problems of self-interest in molecular cell biology or medicine that may require a solution and then search for the most unexpected research directions to solve such challenges while emphasizing the need for newly acquired molecular data.

title: Animal Models of CNS Diseases
fields: Life Sciences (Brain Sciences: Systems, Computational and Cognitive Neuroscience Track)
syllabus:
This course provides an in-depth exploration of different animal and cellular models used in the study of Central Nervous System (CNS) diseases. Through lectures and discussions, students will gain a comprehensive understanding of the current state of various neuropathologies. Each lecture will be given by an expert in the field that will focus on a different CNS disease, delving into the pathologies, symptoms, and phenotypes captured by different models. Students will also learn how these models have contributed to uncovering the underlying mechanisms of the diseases. Moreover, we will discuss the strengths and weaknesses of each model, explore the correlation between animal model and human clinical endpoints in different disorders, and examine potential new directions for the field.
Topics to be covered (please note that lectures 2-12 are not necessarily in the correct order):
• Lecture 1: Introduction A to Animal Models in CNS Research
• Lecture 2: Introduction B from vet perspective + Compassion fatigue
• Lecture 3:  Dementia disorders, with a focus on Alzheimer's Disease
• Lecture 4: Stress, Anxiety and Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)
• Lecture 5: Parkinson's Disease
• Lecture 6: Psychotic disorders including schizophrenia
• Lecture 7: Eating disorders
• Lecture 8: Depression
• Lecture 9: Brain tumor
• Lecture 10: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)
• Lecture 11: Addiction and drug addiction
• Lecture 12: Autism
• Lecture 13: Summary
learning_outcomes: By the end of this course, students will have gained a profound understanding of various CNS diseases and the corresponding animal models, equipping them to critically evaluate scientific literature and contribute to advancements in the field of neuroscience research

title: Bioinformatics
fields: Life Sciences (Computational and Systems Biology Track)
Life Sciences (Molecular and Cellular Neuroscience Track)
syllabus:
This course will teach the data and algorithms behind the most commonly used bioinformatics tools from a biological perspective.  When the course is over, participants should be able to use the data and programs and make informed choices as to the program, the parameters and databases, regardless of the particular site used. Best practices (recommended sites and programs) for various biological contexts will also be taught. In the final project students will take one gene and follow through everything we did in the course on their gene of interest.
Basic topics:
Introduction to Databases
DNA sequencing and assembly
Pairwise comparison
Database similarity searching
Multiple alignment
Motifs, patterns and profiles
Gene Structure
Genome databases and browsers
Additional topics (time permitting):
Comparative genomics
Protein secondary structure
Gene Ontology
Pathway Analysis
Gene knockdown (miRNA, siRNA, and CRISPR)
learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of the course the students will be able to:
• Make informed choices as the programs, parameters and databases to use for solving various biological problems

title: Biology of Metabolism in health and disease
syllabus:
This course is designed to provide students with an in-depth understanding of metabolic regulation in humans and the mechanisms underlying its dysregulation in various physiological and pathological conditions. The course will cover fundamental concepts through key questions related to metabolic regulation, and dysregulation and their contribution to the development of metabolic disorders, such as obesity, diabetes, and metabolic syndrome. Additionally, the course will examine the role of metabolism in aging, cancer, and neurodegenerative diseases.
• How did metabolism evolve? (The origin of metabolism in the deep hydrothermal vents)
• How to assess cell metabolism? (metabolomics, pulse-chase, respirometry)
• Why is glycolysis so essential to red blood cells and neurons? (Hemolytic anemia)
• Why do cancers rely so much on fermentation? (Warburg effect)
• Is the Krebs cycle really a cycle? (anaplerosis and cataplerosis in health and disease)
• How Does Iron Balance the Scales of Health and Disease?
• Circadian clocks and metabolism; who controls whom?
• Why is metabolism correlated with body mass? (BMR, Kleiber’s Law)
• Is exercise really healthy? (AMPK, Creatine Phosphate, PGC-1 alpha)
• Does metabolism control inflammation, or vice versa? (M1, M2 macrophages, Metabolism of dendritic cells and T lymphocytes)
• Is obesity unhealthy? (subcutaneous and visceral fat, inflammation of white adipose tissue)
• Why is obesity associated with diabetes? (Insulin resistance, Type-2-Diabetes, OGTT, hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp)
• What’s the cause of the obesity epidemics and how can it be reduced? (ultraprocessed food, leptin resistance, GLP-1 and its analogues)
• Does metabolism play a role in the development of neurodegenerative diseases?
learning_outcomes:
By the end of the course, students will be able to:
• Understand the principles of metabolic regulation in mammals.
• Analyze the molecular mechanisms involved in metabolic control.
• Evaluate the role of key hormonal signaling in metabolic regulation.
• Identify the causes and consequences of metabolic dysregulation.
• Discuss the relationship between metabolic dysregulation and human diseases.
• Critically analyze current research and advancements in the field.
• Apply acquired knowledge to propose potential therapeutic interventions for metabolic disorders.

title: Biology of Mitochondria and Bioenergetics
syllabus:
Description:
Mitochondria play several roles in eukaryotes: they serve as main suppliers of energy; they are involved in apoptosis, in calcium homeostasis and in iron homeostasis. During the respiratory process, mitochondria produce reactive oxygen species (ROS), which can induce mutations in the mitochondrial DNA, leading to gradual deterioration of tissue function, that is reflected in the ageing process and in diseases associated with aging such as-diabetes, Parkinson and cancer.  The present course will provide a panorama of the physiology of mitochondria, along with its different functions in the cell, emphasizing the contribution of damaged mitochondria to disease.
Aim:
The course intends to provide an up-to-date overview of the field
of mitochondrial research in health and disease.
Objectives:
1. Teach the students about the centrality of mitochondrial research in various fields
of research of biology.
2. Provide tools for understanding and appreciating studies in cellular biology in general and in mitochondrial research in particular.
3. Provide an overview of state of the art techniques in cellular biology.
4. Expose the students to cellular approaches in studying disease, as opposed to more common molecular approaches.
Structure:
The course consists of oral presentations.
Syllabus:
• Introduction: Evolution of mitochondria (the endosymbiotic theory)
• The components of the respiratory chain (respiratory complexes, Proton gradient, ATP synthase)
• Iron Sulfate clusters (essential role in cell viability)
4.   Approaches for studying bioenergetics I: cellular level (ATP, NAD(P)H, respirometry, mitochondrial potential).
5. Approaches for studying bioenergetics II, III: isolated mitochondria, whole organism during rest (direct and indirect calorimetry, BMR, RQ)
6. Brown fat and thermogenesis (Shivering and non-shivering thermogenesis. Brown adipose tissue -UCP1 and its regulation)
7.  Aging and Reactive oxygen species: free radicals, oxidative damage, antioxidant enzymatic mechanisms, role of ROS in aging and in cell signaling
8. Aging and Mitochondrial turnover I: Mitochondrial biogenesis (PGC1 alpha, AMPK)
8. Aging and Mitochondrial turnover II: Mitochondrial clearance )autophagy, mitophagy, mTOR, PINK1, Parkin, Parkinson’s Disease(
9. Mitochondrial dynamics Fusion, fission and their various functions (Mfn1/2, OPA1, DRP1)
10. Mitochondria and apoptosis (cytochrome c)
11. Mitochondrial Ca2+ in physiology and pathology (PTP, NCLX, MCU). Mitochondrial protein import (TOM, TIM complexes)
12. Mitochondrial protein import (Tom and Tim complexes)
13. Mitochondrial DNA (TFAM, haplogroups, heteroplasmy, the mother of all humans: Mitochondrial Eve, identification of the Romanovs)
14. Mitochondrial DNA diseases and therapies (LOHN, Leigh syndrome, MELAS, cybrids)
learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course students should be able to:
1. Evaluate mitochondrial Oxphos function.
2. Analyze respirometry data.
3. Critically read articles related to mitochondrial research.
4. Assess the potential of mitochondrial involvement in disease.

title: Cancer evolution: from mechanisms to treatment
syllabus:
This course will introduce basic and more advanced concepts in of various cellular mechanisms (including cell division, DNA damage and repair, cell signaling and genomics) that can be targeted using anti-cancer therapies.
While doing so, the class will discuss the advantages and disadvantages of different therapeutic approaches, and we will specifically discuss how cancer evolves (addressing clonal evolution vs. acute “big bang” events) to form resistance and think about ways to prevent it.
A critical part of the course is based on active discussion in class to learn principles that guide critical thinking of scientific data. The course is divided into four parts: cell division, DNA damage and repair, cell signaling and genomics. For each part, a scientific paper will be provided, which will be openly discussed at the end of each part.
learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course students will be familiar with up to date concepts in cancer biology, and will develop critical thinking on the emerging topics in the field.

title: Circadian Clocks: Exploring Nature's Timekeepers
syllabus:
Welcome to "Circadian Clocks: Exploring Nature's Timekeepers," an exciting journey into the intricate system of circadian clocks—uncovering how they operate and how we can influence them.
Did you know that nearly every cell in your body has its own clock? These circadian clocks orchestrate a symphony of biological rhythms that influence every aspect; from gene expression to complex physiological processes and behaviour.
We'll begin with introductory lectures providing essential background knowledge. Then, you'll take the lead! You will present an assigned seminal research paper, covering groundbreaking discoveries in circadian biology across various organisms. Following the presentation we will discuss together the paper.
learning_outcomes: By the end of this course, you will gain a circadian perspective to biological questions. Whether you're studying genes, cells, or entire organisms, you'll instinctively consider the "when" alongside the "what" and "how" in your experiments.

title: Clinical, molecular and therapeutic overviews of common types of cancer
syllabus: The course will be delivered by medical oncologists who will share their knowledge and clinical experience. The first lectures will be devoted to basic terms, the hallmarks of cancer and cancer pathology, as well as cancer imaging. Next, we will cover the area of clinical trials: design, terminology, ethical aspects and evaluation of the results. The majority of lectures will be devoted to individual types of cancer, such as brain tumors and breast cancer. Each lecturer will provide the main disease facts such as histological and molecular subtypes, epidemiology and diagnosis. In addition, each presentation will address the current treatments and the burning open questions of relevant research.
learning_outcomes: The students will be exposed to the clinical side of cancer research and decision making by clinicians. Along with this, the students will become familiar with the most prevalent types of cancer and the currently open questions of each disease. We will focus on epidemiology, molecular mechanisms and experimental therapeutics.

title: Cosmic rays and their interactions with the Earth: from geo-atmospheric to medicine research
syllabus:
The Earth system (atmosphere, biosphere, ocean and geosphere) is continuously interacting with the incoming cosmic and solar particles. In this interaction several cosmogenic isotopes are produced and deposited in different archives providing information about climate, biological processes and history. The interpretation of research based on cosmogenic isotopes requires the integration of different scientific fields from physics to medicine. The course will provide an overview of the different applications and  focusing in particular on research at the Weizmann Institute using the Accelerator Mass Spectrometer D-REAMS. Hands-on measurement of environmental/archaeological and medical questions will provide an in-depth understanding of this interdisciplinary field.

16 March Lesson 2: Introduction 2 – Cosmic rays and the earth system: the case of Radiocarbon.
23 March (Purim no lecture)
30 March Lesson 3: Radiocarbon in the biosphere (pollen, phytoliths, seeds, biomarkers): climate/anthropological activities and chronology

Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:
The student will gain an overview and hands-on experience with a wide range of applications of cosmogenic isotopes used in Earth system, atmospheric, archaeological, and medical research. In particular, the system available at the Weizmann Institute will be presented, including an advanced accelerator mass spectrometry system for measuring radiocarbon in samples as small as 10 micrograms.

title: Evolutionary conservation of molecular systems
syllabus:
Syllabus
A 6-lesson (1.5 hours each) course plus an additional meeting for the examination. The course includes lectures, guided examples, discussions, and student seminars. The course consists of two parts. The first part is only theoretical, during which students are exposed to the evolutionary principles that shape molecular systems, with emphasis on microbial immunity, phage host conflicts, and the prokaryotic origins of many immune-related proteins in multicellular organisms. The second part focuses on the functional understanding of proteins, using sequence analysis, structural prediction, conservation, phylogeny, and genomic context, to come up with hypothesis regarding function.
This course explores how modern molecular systems are built on ancient protein parts and mechanisms that originated in bacteria and archaea and were repeatedly reused as life diversified. We begin with the evolutionary framing: what “deep conservation” means, how evolutionary processes such as horizontal gene transfer, gene duplication, and loss reshape biological pathways, and how these principles illuminate complex systems including immune and defense responses across prokaryotes, viruses, and eukaryotes.
The course then shifts from concepts to methods and introduces a practical toolkit for detecting and interpreting conservation in real proteins. Students learn to use UniProt for sequence and functional annotation and to identify domains and motif signatures with InterPro, Pfam, and CDD. They build and interpret multiple sequence alignments, map conservation onto 3D structures, and analyze or predict structures using resources such as the PDB and AlphaFold together with modern structure search and analysis tools.
We focus on why particular features remain conserved, from folds and catalytic or binding pockets to functional surface patches and residue networks that can support allosteric communication. Using immune related proteins as recurring examples, we highlight why these systems are especially informative, because immune genes sit at the front line of continual host pathogen and microbe phage arms races that drive rapid diversification while preserving core mechanisms. We examine how proteins sense triggers, transmit signals, and activate through conformational change. Students compare gradual functional tuning with sequence and learn to translate conservation patterns into mechanistic, testable hypotheses about protein function and regulation. By combining evolutionary theory, comparative genomics, protein databases, and structural reasoning, the course trains students to turn conservation patterns into mechanistic, testable hypotheses about protein function and regulation across the tree of life.
The aim of the course is to provide students with a conceptual and practical framework for understanding how new molecular systems evolve, how protein families diversify, and how uncharacterized proteins can be investigated through the combined use of evolutionary, structural, biochemical, and genomic information.
Student Requirements
Students are expected to attend all course meetings, participate in discussions, and present a short seminar based on scientific literature. Each short presentation will focus on a protein family, immune system, defense mechanism, anti-defense mechanism, or evolutionary theme related to the course. The presentation should emphasize how evolutionary, structural, biochemical, or genomic evidence was used to infer molecular function.
There is no exam. Course completion will be based on attendance, participation, and the student seminar.
learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course students should be able to:
• Microbial life as a source of molecular innovation.
• Phage host arms races and their role in shaping protein evolution.
• The evolutionary relationship between prokaryotic conflict systems and eukaryotic immunity.
• Conservation, diversification, horizontal gene transfer, and protein domain reshuffling.
• Interpretation of multiple sequence alignments, sequence conservation, and conserved motifs.
• AI-based structural prediction using AlphaFold and Structure-based similarity searches.
• Recognition of protein domains, linkers, pockets, catalytic sites and conserved interfaces.
• Integration of sequence, structure, conservation, phylogeny, and genomic context for functional inference.

title: Expanded toolbox for CRISPR-based genome editing

sessions.note: Full schedule is detailed in the comments section,

syllabus:
Expanded toolbox for CRISPR-based genome editing  (course code20273262)
CRISPR-derived technologies have transformed genome engineering by providing robust, programmable, versatile, and increasingly precise tools for modifying DNA and regulating gene function. This laboratory course introduces participants to core methodologies in the field, with emphasis on the most recently expanded toolbox for CRISPR-based genome editing.
Participants will learn how following gene disruption, and homology-directed repair, subsequent innovations expanded the system to include nickases, catalytically inactive Cas proteins, base editors, prime editors, and related CRISPR-derived tools. Special attention will be given to how each technology differs in mechanism, precision, efficiency, delivery requirements, and suitability for specific biological or clinical tasks.
Participants will practice experimental strategies for introducing a single-nucleotide change using CRISPR-Cas ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes combined with a donor repair template for homology-directed repair. This module will highlight the advantages and limitations of RNP delivery, donor design and editing efficiency. In parallel, students will explore and experiment with base editors fused to nickase Cas9 as an alternative strategy for single-base correction without generating double-strand breaks. They will compare cytosine and adenine base editors, examine editing windows, bystander editing, PAM restrictions, and editor compatibility with different types of mutations.
During the bioinformatics sessions, participants will learn to select target sgRNA sequences given the multitude genomic considerations, predict on-target activity, and assess potential off-target sites. They will then apply these principles to the design of genome-editing experiments. The course will also include plasmid construction as a strategy for delivering genome editors and sgRNAs, allowing students to gain experience with the molecular cloning approaches commonly used to assemble CRISPR expression systems. In addition to hands-on laboratory modules, participants will design their own genome-editing project of choice.
The course will also expose participants to the cutting-edge prime editing (PE) approach, which enables targeted insertions, deletions, and base substitutions without requiring double strand breaks or donor templates. Applications of genome editing in model animals will be discussed, including the generation of disease models and functional genetic studies. Finally, the course will address the translation of CRISPR-derived technologies toward human gene therapy, including ethical issues, and regulatory perspectives.
learning_outcomes: Participants will have the opportunity to design a project of their choice, considering in-silico genomic parameters as well as experimental ones. Participants will conduct experiments to achieve knock out and knock in using plasmids, RNP and donor ssDNA as well as most advanced nickase Cas fused to a base editor.

title: Extracellular Matrix Biology: Structure, Remodeling, and Function in Health and Disease
syllabus:
The extracellular matrix (ECM) is a dynamic network of macromolecules that provides structural support to tissues while regulating cell behavior, tissue organization, and organ function through biochemical and biomechanical signaling.
The course begins with the fundamentals of ECM composition, assembly, and architecture, and then moves on to ECM remodeling and cell–ECM interactions, with an introduction to experimental approaches, including imaging and omics-based analyses. A substantial part of the course focuses on how ECM dynamics, driven by cross-linking enzymes and matrix-degrading enzymes such as matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), shape the biochemical and mechanical properties of the matrix and influence development, repair, inflammation, and disease. The course also examines the role of the ECM in a range pathological processes including fibrosis, cancer, biomineralization, and cholesterol crystallization. Special attention will be given to ECM biological memory, which reflects the ability of the matrix to preserve tissue history and influence future cell behavior, repair, and disease progression. The course concludes by exploring the ECM as a source of disease biomarkers and as a target for next-generation therapeutics and regenerative medicine.
learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will have a comprehensive understanding of the composition, organization, and dynamic remodeling of the extracellular matrix (ECM) and its roles in maintaining tissue homeostasis and in disease. They will be able to integrate molecular, cellular, and biomechanical aspects of ECM biology, interpret findings obtained using modern experimental approaches, and discuss how ECM remodeling contributes to pathological processes such as fibrosis, cancer, and biomineralization. Students will also recognize the potential of the ECM and its remodeling enzymes as sources of diagnostic biomarkers and as therapeutic targets in regenerative medicine and precision healthcare.

title: Frontiers of Molecular Membrane Biology
syllabus:
Biological membranes are essential for life. They form cells and organelles and enable the separation and the formation of unique domains. Membranes control the content of a cell by means of selective permeability and control the flow of messages between intracellular domains by sending, receiving and processing information in the form of chemical and electrical signals. Cells, organelles and vesicles must also acquire, maintain and modify their shape and composition to jointly fulfil a plethora of important physiological functions ranging from neuronal transmission to fertilization and muscle contraction.
During this course we will discuss fundamental cell biology processes that involve membrane remodeling:
Organelle biogenesis, function and dynamics (Fusion, division and trafficking).
Vesicular trafficking through the endocytic pathway.
Protein targeting, insertion and translocation.
Vesicular secretion, exosomes and extracellular vesicles.
Intracellular communication via membrane contact sites.
The course will focus on recent research and novel findings, beyond the scope of existing textbooks, in the fields of organellar biology and membrane remodeling.
learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course:
• Students will be familiar with up to date research topics and methods in organellar and cell biology.
• Students will be able to demonstrate understanding of current issues in cell biology and improved skills in critically evaluating scientific papers in this field.

title: Gene expression profiling: a practical course for RNA library preparation ready for sequencing
syllabus:
Understanding biological systems using state-of-the-art genomics methods require, among other approaches, the gene expression profiling of different tissues, states, or conditions. RNA-seq is the method of choice to study gene expression with little background noise and a large dynamic range for detection of differentially expressed genes. This laboratory course will provide hands-on training on bulk MARS-seq, a method for digital gene expression analysis developed in Ido Amit lab at the Weizmann Institute. This protocol is designed for preparation of 3’ RNA sequencing libraries from low input RNA material in a simple, cost-effective fashion, due to early multiplexing of the samples. Libraries prepared in the course will be sequenced and analyzed. In order to enable fast and user-friendly data analysis, the LSCF Bioinformatics unit developed an intuitive and scalable transcriptome pipeline (UTAP) that executes the full process on Weizmann computer cluster (WEXAC), starting from sequences and ending with a comprehensive report. The sequenced data analysis part will be included in a session (2 hours) that will cover the theoretical basis for the analysis steps UTAP performs and a hands-on session to run the pipeline and understand the outputs it produces.
During the course, we will also present and discuss key aspects of genomics research, the power of unbiased gene expression profiling and Next Generation Sequencing (NGS), as well as quality control evaluation of input material, libraries and sequenced samples.
learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course students should be able to:
• Demonstrate an understanding of the notion of NGS technologies
• Demonstrate knowledge of RNA-seq technologies in general, including input requirements
• Demonstrate an understanding of molecular biology processes in the process of RNA-seq library preparation
• Generate RNA-seq libraries from limiting amounts of RNA, ready to be sequenced in any available Illumina sequencer.
• Demonstrate familiarity with data resulting from Illumina platforms

title: Global Change in Marine Ecosystems
syllabus:
Global Change in Marine Ecosystems   (course code20273411)
Marine environments are experiencing significant environmental changes, a result of global changes. The aim of this course is to expose students to the processes taking place and the threats to habitats in marine environments following climate change. What are the trends and what are the ecological, sociological, and economic implications? We will deal with issues of problems and solutions to the major threats to marine habitats.
Course Structure
This intensive 6-day course will be taught in the waters of the Gulf of Aqaba and in laboratory and will include lectures given by experts in the field, a short research project, presentation of articles in the field and guided tours. Students will be asked to read a variety of selected texts as well as a series of contemporary scientific articles.
Key topics covered in the course
•
Impact of climate change in the marine environment.
•
The coral reef under global and local changes.
•
Seagrasses response to global changes.
•
Ecological, physiological and behavioral responses of marine organisms under climatic changes.
•
Rising sea level.
•
Ocean acidification.
•
Invading species.
•
Warming and bleaching corals, possible solutions: minimizing changes, acclimatization and adaptation.
The Grade Structure
•
Journal club (15%)
•
Two (2) written exams to be held during the course (40%).
•
Presentation of group projects (20%)
•
Group Project Report (25%). The written report is submitted 4 weeks after the course ends.

title: Hands-on Data Analysis and Statistics for the Life Sciences
syllabus:
The course spans two semesters and is organized into six instructional modules. Each module is taught over four weeks:
Week 1: Lecture introducing the statistical concepts and their biological motivation.
Weeks 2–3: Hands-on computational project analyzing real biological datasets.
Week 4: Project-based quiz assessing conceptual understanding and practical data analysis skills.
The course concludes with a comprehensive final examination.
Course Topics
1. Probability and Descriptive Statistics
Introduction to probability, common probability distributions, descriptive statistics, sampling, and variability in biological data.
2. Statistical Estimation
Parameter estimation, uncertainty quantification, confidence intervals, and statistical inference from experimental measurements.
3. Correlation and Multivariable Data Analysis
Methods for quantifying relationships between variables, including correlation analysis and approaches for analyzing spatial patterns in biological data.
4. Statistical Inference
Hypothesis testing, resampling methods, statistical power, multiple hypothesis testing, and interpretation of statistical significance.
5. Regression Analysis
Linear and nonlinear regression, model fitting, analysis of variance, model assumptions, and evaluation of predictive models.
6. Clustering and Exploratory Data Analysis
Unsupervised methods for identifying patterns and structure in complex biological datasets and exploratory analysis of high-dimensional data.
learning_outcomes:
1. Analyze biological datasets using appropriate statistical methods.
2. Critically evaluate statistical evidence in biological research.
3. Apply computational tools to perform reproducible data analyses and communicate statistically sound conclusions from experimental data.

title: High Impact Scientific Writing
syllabus: A workshop-style course on scientific writing for PhD students that are ready to transform their research projects into high-impact scientific journal articles. Participants should ideally have a research project that is advanced enough to be written up. The course focuses on structuring and writing journal articles through the narrative lens. There are short weekly writing assignments that enable students to implement the principles we learn in class. Limited enrollment.
learning_outcomes: Students who complete this writing workshop will (1) be able to implement a variety of strategies for improving effective writing behavior, (2) understand the canonical structure of a scientific manuscript, (3) be able to craft a scientific story and understand how to develop the canonical sections of their scientific manuscript to support their story, (4) understand the publication process for scientific manuscripts, and (5) be able to write about their manuscript for a lay audience.

title: High throughput assay methodologies
syllabus:
• Introduction to research methodologists in drug discovery
• Guidelines for assays, screening methods
• General concepts for biochemical and cell-based assays.
• Target identification
• Phenotypic vs targeted drug discovery
• Lab exercises for proteases and viability screening
• Emerging strategies in drug discovery
Project proposal:
Participants will experience hands-on training sessions using experimental methods to provide a foundation for applying in-vitro approaches in drug discovery.
The course takes place at the INCPM, drug discovery facility.
The course will focus on high throughput screening methodologist for small molecules and their use as chemical probes or leads to novel drugs.
Students will perform different types of experiments demonstrating assay development and screening methods and will practice interpreting their data.
Lectures will provide background for lab experiments and broader knowledge of research strategies.
Finally, each group of students will choose a target of their interest and will prepare a research proposal as a short presentation for the class, using the tools they acquired during the course.
learning_outcomes: During the course, students will learn about principles, methods and goals of high throughput screening as it pertains to driving academic research towards applications relevant to the clinic. The scope of the course will be limited to small molecules and their use as chemical probes or leads to novel drugs. Students will perform different types of the experiments demonstrating assay development and screening methods, and will practice interpreting their data. Lectures will provide background for lab experiments and broader knowledge of strategies such as phenotypic screening. Data sharing and multidisciplinary team-work is central to drug discovery, so students will perform a team-based exercise using open-source data from an antiviral discovery campaign. Finally, students will present project proposals for review in a group exercise.

title: History and Philosophy, Intelligence and Computing
fields: Life Sciences (Brain Sciences: Systems, Computational and Cognitive Neuroscience Track)
syllabus:
This is a interdisciplinary course showing the relevance of the humanities to cutting-edge technologies, such as Artificial Intelligence. This relevance is to the core concern of developing novel algorithms, not peripheral (like Ethical issues).
This course presents a history of ideas relating to computing and Artificial Intelligence, beginning with the pre-Socratic philosophers, going through an overview of existing AI, and ending with blueprints for future programming, with videos of example runs. The course can also serve as an introduction to the history of ideas, using computation and AI as an example.
Opening
•
Introduction – How can we “think outside the box”? Examining unspoken assumptions. What are History and Philosophy? Introduction to the two fields using the story of Positivism form the French revolution, via Auguste Comte to current secular thought.
•
Overview, Dreams, Background – Overview – the interaction between 3 carriers of intelligence. Dreams - The fascination with thinking machines from ancient theologies through medieval Islam into some failed attempts of the 19th and early 20th century. Background - Pan-computational theories, catching up on logic, mathematics and algorithms.
Cultural Background
•
Rationalism – About “isms”. The temptation to over-simplify. The irrational belief that rationality (Logic, Mathematics) will solve all problems.
•
Science and Secularization – The rise of modern critical thinking (Protestantism). The canonical story of the evolution of modern astronomy. The myth of a “scientific clean sweep” (Descartes and Bacon). The rise of science up to scientific psychology (1913).
•
The Modern Mindset - Kant and the Analytic-Continental split. Recap reformation and enlightenment. Romanticism and the Victorian era. Recap of Positivism and WW1. Modernism: Focusing on efficiency, from architecture to agriculture. The rise of the MBA way of thinking (Simon).
The rise of AI
•
Pre-AI fields – Mathematics: state automata, boolean logic. Cybernetics: Tortoises, Punched cards, telegraph. Psychology and Linguistics: Behaviourism, review of Cognitive psychology and Linguistics. Electrical engineering: oscilloscopes and telephone exchanges. Biology – Neural networks (1943).
•
USA in the 1940-70s - birth of computation and AI – Freedom of will (Weber & Andersen). WW2: America’s self image as sanity between the Nazis and Communists, Vietnam War and the Cold-war philosophy. Von Neumann and the first computers. Cognitive revolution, founding AI: Dartmouth conference of 1956.
Overview of AI
•
GOFAI – Good, Old-Fashioned, Artificial Intelligence – Definitions of Intelligence and AI. Logic, Fuzz, and experts. IBM, open-source. Herbert Simon’s pivotal role. Checkers, Chess, Go. Eliza. Winograd’s SHRDLU. The Nuclear bomb in the background.
•
Turing Test and problems with knowledge – Turing (1950). Variants and criticisms. Was it a joke? “Common sense” etc. The fear of X taking over from humanity. CYC. Knowledge that vs knowledge how. Atomism and rationalism. Knowledge as true, justified belief and the infinite regress of “justified justifications”.
•
Biologically-inspired AI – Passive walking robots. Genetic Algorithms. Neural nets. Deep learning / Big Data. Simulating insects (Brooks). GPT. Histomimetic robotics – Hockings.
Critiques of AI
•
Phenomenology (Dreyfus) – Philosophical background: phenomenology and existentialism. Heidegger. Three broken promises of AI, four assumptions necessary for AI, four distinctions, skills, sweeping pessimism. A fateful game of Chess. First-step fallacy.
•
Other Critiques – Replies to Dreyfus. Intelligence embedded and embodied. Winograd & Flores (1986). Visions of the future: Singularity, trans-humanism. Optimism and Pessimism. Fiction inspiring technology.
Future Directions and Conclusion
•
Post-rationalist AI – Technology vs Science. Human-like vs Rational AI. Papert. Anthropic AI. Subjectivity and Introspection. Legitimacy issues. A-priori causes for optimism. Steps for developing introspection-based algorithms. Examples + implementation videos.
•
Ethics and Conclusion – Ethics and Technophobia: Technology as a threat to workers, and to religions. Technology changing human thought. The future arriving prematurely (Toffler). Current social problems: leaks, social control, perpetuation of prejudices (in big data). AI safely.
Conclusion – a synchronous review of the intellectual background to AI.

title: Human Evolution
fields: Life Sciences (Brain Sciences: Systems, Computational and Cognitive Neuroscience Track)
syllabus:
How did humans come to be? What sets us apart from the other human species we used to live side by side with? And why are we the last human standing?
In this course, we will explore human evolution, from its anthropological and archaeological aspects (fossils, stone tools, cave paintings, and more) to its genetic and molecular basis. We will focus on the ancient DNA revolution and how it provided unprecedented access to the genetic changes that shaped human lineages. We will study the processes that shape our evolution, from positive selection through admixture to speciation, and the computational and genomic methods to detect these processes.
The final six meetings will be devoted to student seminars of key advances, concepts, and open questions in human evolution.
learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of the course students will be able to:
1. Demonstrate broad familiarity with research topics and open questions in human evolution
2. Understand the multiple genetic and phenotypic layers of evolutionary changes
3. Critically assess current methodologies and important findings in the field
4. Demonstrate improved skills in critically evaluating scientific papers

title: Introduction to Disruptive Science
syllabus:
In science, the ultimate achievement is a breakthrough that reshapes knowledge and redefines the field. Of course, a breakthrough can also significantly boost your career.
But what are the skills and methodologies required to achieve that goal? We believe the key lies in learning from the startup world, where breakthroughs and disruption are the primary objectives.
This course aims to help you acquire disruption skills, methodologies and mindsets that originate from the startup ecosystem, but have been tailored to the research environment. The course is based on long-term research and was refined with the experience gained in many acceleration courses and workshops.
Our goal is to introduce you to a new mindset of “thinking in terms of disruption” and guide you in testing disruption techniques on your own research.
The course includes 7 main topics:
• Introduction to Disruptive Science – How and when scientific breakthroughs appear, how to move out of the research’s comfort zone.
• Disruptive Checklist – How to test the disruptiveness of a research project, and how to steer it in that direction.
• Breakthrough Brainstorming – How to adjust hi-tech-related brainstorming and opportunity-search methodologies to research.
• Agile Research – How to realign research projects towards disruption.
• Disruptive Mindset – How to seek and leverage research opportunities, how to lead research on less-certain grounds.
• Forefront Collaboration – New ways to create and maintain collaboration at the forefront of a research discipline.
• Promoting Disruptive Research – How to promote research ideas and findings that are non- standard.
In terms of assignments, you will be asked to write approximately one page following each of the topics – testing the topic at hand against your research. The lectures will include reflection sessions, in which we will comment on and discuss these applications. The final assignment will compile these tests and insights into an analysis of your research in disruptive terms.
learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course, students will:
• Have a clear view on Disruptive Science – How it differs from incremental progression and where to look for breakthrough leverage.
• Acquire and practice disruptive-thinking skills that empower disruptive scientists, among them: Disruption Checklist, Disruptive Mindset, collaboration and promotion of breakthrough research.
• Test disruption methodologies on their own research.

title: Introduction to Embryonic Development: Foundations and Principles
syllabus:
Embryonic development is an extraordinary generative process, starting at the microscopic level and culminating in the formation of a fully developed organism on a macroscopic scale. We all begin life as a single fertilized egg, yet within weeks, we develop into complex multicellular organisms with defined body axes, specialized cell types, and functional organs capable of interacting intricately with our environment. How does this transformation occur? how do complex structures form from simple ones? how do identical cells acquire different fates and how do body axes form in symmetric embryos? why do embryos of different species look so similar?
In this course, we will explore these fundamental questions. We'll start by examining the major breakthroughs in developmental biology that have shaped our current understanding. You will learn how complex body structures emerge through the patterning and growth of simpler forms, how cell types diversify, and the role of genes and their regulation in these processes. We will also delve into how researchers use various animal models to study development, what can and cannot be learned from in-vitro models, and the classic as well as cutting-edge tools used in the field.
learning_outcomes:
By the end of this course, students will have acquired the following knowledge and skills:
•
Students will learn the connections between developmental biology and species evolution, appreciate how our knowledge of development has advanced through the contributions of prominent researchers, and appreciate the similarities and differences in developmental strategies across various species.
•
Understand key events in embryonic development such as fertilization, gastrulation, segmentation etc.
•
Develop a comprehensive understanding of how embryonic development is regulated through gene expression, morphogenesis, and tissue organizing centers, as well as how disruptions in these processes can affect organism health and viability.
•
Gain familiarity with both classic and cutting-edge techniques used in developmental biology research.

title: Introduction to Neuroscience: Molecular Neuroscience - Genes to Behavior
fields: Life Sciences (Brain Sciences: Systems, Computational and Cognitive Neuroscience Track)
Life Sciences (Molecular and Cellular Neuroscience Track)
syllabus:
One of the foremost challenges in neuroscience is to establish a causal relationship between an animal’s genetic make-up and its behavior: while it seems clear that certain normal and pathological behavioral traits have a genetic basis, understanding how genes determine the function of neurons and neural circuits to thereby generate and modulate an animal’s behavior is highly challenging and requires an integrated view of nearly all disciplines in neuroscience. In this course, we will present basic concepts on multiple levels of nervous system organization & function and discuss how they are connected to each other.
The syllabus will include the following topics:
- Evolution of the brain and animal behavior: innate versus adaptive behavior
- Neurogenetics - the hereditary basis of behavioral traits
- Genomic & transcriptional regulation in neurons
- Epigenetics and transgenerational inheritance of behavioral traits
- Cell biology of neurons: cellular diversity
- Neural circuits: assembly, from micro- to meso-scale circuit function
- Experience-dependent plasticity: Different forms of cellular and circuit plasticity, learning & memory
- C.elegans as a model system for molecular and systems neuroscience
- From genes to sexual behavior
learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course students should be able to:
• Demonstrate proficiency in the unique properties of brain cells, their diversity and their different roles within brain circuits.
• Understand the basic processes governing the assembly and function of neural circuits.
• Understand the processes of neural plasticity at the synaptic, cellular and circuit levels.
• Become familiar with modern concepts and techniques in cellular and circuit neuroscience and be able to read and understand current literature.

title: Introduction to Neuroscience: Systems Neuroscience
fields: Life Sciences (Brain Sciences: Systems, Computational and Cognitive Neuroscience Track)
syllabus:
The brain underlies our ability to perceive, move, remember, think. This course will introduce students to the major systems of the brain, which underlie these abilities, focusing on sensory, motor and memory systems. The course will start with classical "textbook" concepts and methods in the field of Systems Neuroscience, but will then emphasize contemporary approaches, concepts and debates.
REMARK: As is the case for most of the Brain Sciences courses at Weizmann, the students in this course come from heterogeneous backgrounds, including biology, physics, computer science, psychology, and engineering. Some of the course material may be familiar to students who took neuroscience courses during their undergraduate studies ; but the more advanced material in this course will be well beyond the scope of typical undergraduate courses. We will provide book chapters as background reading, these chapters will serve as a refresher reading for those students that did learn some neuroscience in the past, and will be a must-read for those students who have no background at all in neuroscience (see more below). No special mathematical knowledge is required for this course.
Syllabus (week by week):
Overview of brain systems and general principles of their functional organization: From cortical maps and subcortical loops to the micro-structure of brain circuits and their interconnections. Brief introduction to Methodologies used to study brain systems (Ulanovsky)
Moving: Movement generation – Peripheral and central processes. (Paz)
Seeing: Peripheral visual processes. (Rivlin)
Seeing: Central visual processes. (Malach)
Smelling and tasting: Peripheral and central processes. (Sobel)
Hearing (and balance): Peripheral and central processes. (Ulanovsky)
Mechanisms of stimulus feature selectivity in sensory systems. (Lampl)
Touching: Peripheral and central processes. (Ahissar)
Active sensing: Closing motor-sensory loops. (Ahissar)
Looking and seeing: mind-body interactions between periphery, brainstem and cortex. (Barash)
Remembering: Overview of memory systems. (Dudai)
Learning: Basal ganglia. (Rivlin)
Learning: The cerebellum in motor learning and cognition. (Eyal Cohen)
Modulating: Neuromodulatory systems of the brain (Kawashima)
Integrating: The prefrontal cortex.  (Yizhar)
Integrating: The hippocampus in spatial navigation and memory consolidation. (Ulanovsky)
learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course students should be be able to:
• Describe different brain systems, starting with basic historical findings and concepts, and ending with advanced-level current results and theories.
• Demonstrate sufficient knowledge required to take more advanced courses in systems neuroscience.

title: Marine microbiology
syllabus:
Marine microbiology  (course code20273512)
The course includes a preparatory meeting of lectures, introduction to projects and information for “journal clubs”. The meeting will take place on Sunday, March 27, 2022, 09:00-18:00, online via ZOOM or at one of the universities in central Israel. All participants must attend.
10 days at Eilat with emphasis on group projects as well as lectures on selected topics, research cruises, tours and "journal clubs".
A summary meeting at one of the universities in the center of the country to present data and conclusions and submit projects’ reports.
Marine microbiology is a major topic in oceanography and marine biology. Microorganisms (bacteria, algae, phages, protists) make up most of the biomass at sea, activate geochemical cycles, are major prey in the open water and sea floor food webs, are involved in the bleaching process, and have symbiotic relationships with animals.
The course provides the tools for understanding the status of the micro world in the macro world:
Methods for sampling, isolation and enrichment, identification and quantification of microorganisms; Various environments such as open water, hypersaline pools and microbial mats; Use of molecular tools for characterizing populations and determining their physiological state; Oceanographic processes, primary and secondary production; Regulation of microbial physiology and adaptation to environmental stresses; Relation with global changes and human impact on marine systems.
The grade structure
The course grade will be based on:
Journal club presentation  (30%)
Evaluation on the work on the research project  (35%)
Presentation of the project results and the final report on the project (35%). The report is submitted at the summary meeting that will be held after the completion of the course in coordination with the students.

title: Mathematics for biologists
fields: Life Sciences (Brain Sciences: Systems, Computational and Cognitive Neuroscience Track)
Life Sciences (Computational and Systems Biology Track)
syllabus:
The course will introduce students who come from a non-mathematical background to basic mathematical tools that are essential for much of today's biological research: differential equations, linear algebra and linear systems theory, and a brief introduction to Fourier analysis. The intention is to provide a firm mathematical background for applications to be covered in advanced courses in Systems Biology and in Theoretical Neuroscience.
Topics to be covered:
• Introduction to differential equations.
• First-order ordinary differential equations: linear equations, separable equations, modeling with first-order equations, equilibrium solutions. Examples of applications include: RC circuits and current-integration by neurons.
• Introduction to linear algebra: Matrix and vector operations.
• Determinants.
• Systems of linear equations.
• Linear transformations.
• Matrix diagonalization. Systems of linear differential equations, Relation of matrix diagonalization to solutions of systems of differential equations. Examples of applications include: predator-prey interactions.
• Inner product spaces.
• Orthogonal and orthonormal bases.
• Introduction to Fourier analysis.
learning_outcomes: Familiarity with basic mathematical tools that are essential for much of today's biological research: ordinary differential equations, linear algebra and linear systems theory, and a brief introduction to Fourier analysis. Knowledge sufficient to provide a mathematical background for applications to be covered in advanced courses in Systems Biology and in Theoretical Neuroscience.

Demonstrate knowledge in a wide range of neuroscience methods.
Read and understand research papers that utilize modern molecular approaches, neurophysiology, and imaging techniques.
Conduct experiments and analyze data using electrophysiology and optical imaging.

title: Microsurgery for studying physiology and cancer in mice
syllabus:
The absence of formal training in surgical principles can lead to a lack of understanding of the equal significance of both technically correct surgery and pre- and post-operative care of animals. Consideration of both the surgery itself and the peri-operative care of animals will result in an increase in animal welfare and the quality of data obtained from the surgical model. For example, subclinical post-surgical infection can confound results, as can changes in behavior and physiology seen with pain. This course will help to build a strong foundation of knowledge and skill in rodent surgery and allow to train on simple procedures. We will learn about rodent surgery best practice, pre-and postoperative care, ondemand surgical techniques, and animal welfare in the surgical setting Topics
Theoretical: 1. Principles of Surgical Asepsis 2. Surgical Instrumentation, Care and Handling of Surgical Equipment 3. Biomaterials, glues, clips, suture materials and Suture Patterns 4. Preoperative, Intraoperative and postoperative Care 5. Preparation of the Operative Site 6. Wounds and basic principles of wound management, and bleeding control 7. Principles of Anesthesia and analgesia under experimental constraints 8. Surgical Infections and Antibiotic Selection (experimental limitations) 9. Model specific topographic anatomy
Practical: Hands-on training based on attendees needs and tips and tricks for the techniques of interest Basic non surgical procedures (intubation, gavage, iv injection, blood collection, intra-articular injections, intrathecal injection) Surgical procedures, examples: intra-cranial injection, Head post implantation, transplantation under the kidney capsule, nephrectomy, splenectomy, catheterization CSF collection,  Orthotopic transplantation models: pancreas, mammary fat pad, prostate

title: Molecular and Cellular Bases of Cancer: Mutations, the Microenvironment, Immunology and Therapies
fields: Life Sciences (Computational and Systems Biology Track)
Life Sciences (Molecular and Cellular Neuroscience Track)
syllabus: This course will provide a comprehensive overview of the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying cancer initiation, progression, and treatment. It will cover the normal regulation of cell proliferation, survival, differentiation, and genome integrity, including cell cycle control, DNA damage responses, and signal transduction pathways. It will then examine how oncogenes, tumor suppressor genes, mutations, chromosomal instability, and epigenetic alterations drive malignant transformation. Special emphasis is placed on tumor heterogeneity, clonal evolution, and mechanisms of metastasis and therapy resistance. The role of the tumor microenvironment (TME), growth factors, inflammation, angiogenesis, and tumor–immune interactions will be discussed in depth. The course will further review major therapeutic strategies, including chemotherapy, radiotherapy, targeted therapies such as tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), monoclonal antibodies, immune checkpoint blockers (ICBs), and emerging therapeutic approaches including T cell engagers, degraders and combination therapies. Through selected examples from breast, lung, and other cancers, students will gain an integrated understanding of modern cancer biology, immunotherapy and precision oncology.
learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course students should be able to:
• Explain the fundamental principles of cancer biology, including the multistep nature of tumorigenesis and the hallmarks of cancer.
• Describe the molecular mechanisms by which oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes regulate cell behavior, and explain how their alterations contribute to malignant transformation.
• Analyze the signaling pathways that control cell proliferation, survival, differentiation, and metabolism, including pathways mediated by RTKs, RAS, PI3K-AKT, and p53.
• Evaluate the mechanisms that maintain genomic integrity, and explain how defects in DNA repair and chromosome maintenance promote cancer development.
• Interpret the roles of the tumor microenvironment in cancer progression, including stromal cells, immune cells, extracellular matrix, and angiogenesis.
• Explain the biological basis of invasion and metastasis, including epithelial–mesenchymal transition, dissemination, and colonization of distant organs.
• Assess the contribution of tumor heterogeneity, clonal evolution, and clonal selection to cancer progression and therapeutic resistance.
• Describe the interactions between cancer and the immune system, and evaluate the principles underlying cancer immunotherapy.
• Compare conventional, targeted, and immune-based cancer therapies, and explain the molecular mechanisms responsible for therapeutic response or resistance.
• Critically evaluate cancer research literature and integrate experimental evidence into current models of cancer biology.
• Apply concepts from cancer genetics, signaling, and tumor evolution to clinical case studies, including precision oncology approaches.
• Formulate mechanistic hypotheses and experimental strategies to address unresolved questions in cancer research.
• Critically assess emerging concepts in cancer biology, such as tumor plasticity, cancer stem cells, extrachromosomal circular DNA (ecDNA), and adaptive resistance networks.

title: Raising and killing the messengers: The post-transcriptional fate of mRNAs and other long RNAs
syllabus:
The information for creating proteins is stored in cells in the form of DNA, but the genome remains a useless blueprint without transcription into messenger RNA molecules (mRNAs) and other, less well understood long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs). This process is subjected to extensive regulatory processes, which are critical in order to ensure precise expression of the specific repertoire of proteins establishing cell-type–specific identity. Some of the most fascinating forms of regulation are applied to mRNA following transcription, and these have dramatic effects on the identity and the quantity of the protein that will eventually be produced. These regulatory pathways have not only been implicated as the molecular mechanisms underlying multiple human diseases, but are also increasingly adopted as a strategy for therapeutic intervention. In this course we will explore all the major points of control during the life trajectory of an mRNA, and discuss the functional outcomes of their impairment. Topics will include splicing, polyadenylation, export from the nucleus, localization to cellular bodies, translation, and decay. We will also discuss RNAi and its therapeutic uses, and long noncoding RNAs that do no encode proteins. We will learn about both traditional and cutting edge approaches for studying the transcriptome at different resolutions, as well as computational and statistical methods for interpreting the data they generate. Emphasis will be put on designing and critically interpreting experiments.
We expect to cover the following topics (typically one topic a week):
• Constitutive and alternative splicing
• Determination of 3' ends by cleavage and polyadenylation
• Export from nucleus to cytosol
• mRNA degradation
• Nonsense mediated decay
• mRNA localization in the cytoplasm
• Translational control
• RNA interference
• RNA editing and other modifications
• Long noncoding RNAs and their deviations from mRNAs
• Circular RNAs
• Processing of long RNAs into microRNAs and other small RNAs
learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of the course students will be able to:
• Demonstrate broad familiarity with research topics and open questions in RNA field
• Discuss both traditional and high-throughput methods for studying RNAs
• Demonstrate improved skills in critically evaluating scientific papers

title: Real-Time and Digital PCR for the Detection of Low-Copy-Number Targets According to MIQE Guidelines

sessions.note: Full schedule is detailed in the comments section,

syllabus:
Real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR) is a robust, widely used, and routine method for the detection and quantification of nucleic acids. The design, execution, analysis, and publication of qPCR experiments should comply with the Minimum Information for Publication of Quantitative Real-Time PCR Experiments guidelines, known as the MIQE guidelines (Bustin et al., 2009). In this course, participants will plan, perform, and statistically analyse qPCR experiments according to these established standards.
A major challenge in qPCR is the reliable detection and quantification of rare targets present at low copy number in biological samples. Course participants will gain practical experience in analysing gene expression under such demanding conditions, including absolute quantification of a small RNA (miR). Two main experimental strategies for improving detection and quantification of low-copy-number targets will be addressed. First, participants will prepare cDNA, perform pre-amplification, carry out qPCR, and analyse the resulting data. Second, they will examine the principles, advantages, and limitations of digital PCR (dPCR) as an alternative approach.
Digital PCR is particularly valuable when precise and sensitive nucleic acid quantification is required, including for low-abundance targets, rare mutations, copy-number variation, pathogen detection, and validation of qPCR results, especially in cases where pre-amplification has not been performed. In dPCR, the sample is partitioned into thousands of independent reactions, and amplification is scored as positive or negative in each partition. Target concentration is then calculated statistically. The key advantages of dPCR include absolute quantification without the need for a standard curve, high analytical sensitivity, strong precision at low target concentrations, and enhanced detection of small fold changes or rare variants in complex samples.
A substantial component of the course will be devoted to in silico data analysis and the application of appropriate statistical methods for qPCR data interpretation.
learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of the course “qPCR by the MIQE guidelines and dPCR” students should be able to:
• Discuss the use of real-time PCR as a reliable and sensitive method for quantifying nucleic acids and its applications according to the MIQE guidelines.
• Discuss algorithms for primer design.
• Experiment (hands on) to get relative quantification of selected cellular mRNAs at low copy number using pre-amplification followed by qPCR.
• Collect data as well as differentiate between the various methods of analysis.
• Discuss the need for suitable standards to guide proper practice and data communication. In this regard, appreciate the need to adhere to the well-defined MIQE (Minimum standard for publication of qPCR Experiments) criteria.
• Obtain and appreciate tools for statistical analysis.
• Translate the acquired the knowledge. Thus, allow to adapt, in one’s own systems of choice, proper technical and analytical methodologies that are reliably used in real-time PCR.
• Appreciate Digital PCR (dPCR), its applications and advantages as well as limitations.

title: Reef Fish Neurobiology
syllabus:
Reef Fish Neurobiology  (course code20273421)
This course provides an integrative exploration of the neural and physiological mechanisms driving the behavior of coral reef fish. Designed for advanced undergraduate and graduate students, the curriculum bridges the gap between fundamental brain sciences and marine fish ecology. We will examine brain genetics and anatomy, regulatory neuronal circuits, and embryonic development alongside complex behavioral traits, including social dynamics, rhythmic cycles, sleep and reproduction. Through a combination of theoretical lectures, field and lab projects, students will master experimental strategies, data acquisition and analysis techniques. By the end of the course, participants will have gained the knowledge, practical skills and conceptual framework necessary to conduct advanced neurobiological research in various reef fish and diverse marine environments.
Course Structure
A 6-day course. The course includes lectures, labs & practical: projects & hands-on exercises, in situ data collection, data simulation, labs and demonstrations, student presentations.
Main topics
1.   Neuroethology & Circuitry: Brain anatomy, neuronal circuit mapping, and the neural basis of complex behaviors in fish.
2.   Chronobiology: Molecular and cellular mechanisms of sleep, circadian rhythms, and the impact of light (photoreception) on fish behavior.
3.   Ecological Ichthyology: Fish diversity, speciation, and the evolutionary transition from larvae to adults in the Red Sea.
4.   Functional Morphology: The biomechanics of feeding, swimming, and the physiological adaptations of reef fish.
5.   Social & Behavioral Ecology: Mechanisms of social interaction, navigation, and group dynamics in coral reef environments.
6.   Applied Marine Biology: Fundamentals of aquaculture, fish physiology, and conservation strategies for marine ecosystems.
7. Experimental Methodology: High-resolution imaging, data acquisition, and field-based research techniques.
The research projects in the course will focus on the following topics:
1. The effect of artificial light pollution on sleep.
2. Social behavior of clown fish.
3. Development of the nervous system in larvae.
4. Interaction of cleaner fish with fish guests.
5. The effect of divers versus a marine robot on fish behavior and diversity.
The grade structure
Presentations 50%
Final exam 50%
learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course students should be able to:
1. Quantitative biological analysis. Formulate and address quantitative questions regarding neural circuits, physiological processes, and the rhythmic behaviors (such as sleep and circadian cycles) of coral reef fish in response to marine environmental stimuli.
2. Environmental impact assessment. Analyze how fluctuating environmental conditions, including light, temperature, and habitat complexity, affect the neural activity, behavioral phenotypes, and physiological performance of marine fish.
3. Experimental design in fish neurobiology. Design robust experimental strategies and field protocols for observing and recording neural activity, embryonic development, and social interactions within both controlled marine laboratory settings and in-situ reef environments.
4. Advanced data processing. Process and calibrate raw biological data, utilizing modern techniques such as high-resolution imaging, behavioral tracking, and physiological sensors, to obtain biologically and ecologically meaningful quantities.
5. Technical trade-off evaluation. Evaluate trade-offs in the selection and deployment of research technologies, such as choosing between various imaging systems, molecular tools, or behavioral platforms.
6. Scientific interpretation and communication. Interpret, synthesize, and present complex neurobiological data to support scientific conclusions regarding the evolution, diversity, and conservation of fish brain-behavior systems in diverse marine environments.

syllabus: The Scientific Writing Course for MSc and PhD students in the Life Sciences provides the tools necessary for writing coherent, well-organized research papers, posters, presentations and other documents.
