• Explain the organization of a thesis/ paper/ research proposal, and the rationale behind these conventions
• Practice writing the various sections of a research paper
• Recall common mistakes and how to avoid them
• Use techniques for effective scientific writing (papers, posters, presentations, thesis, CV etc.)
• Engage in scientific communication with confidence

title: Single-Cell Genomics: Experimental Methods and Data Analysis

sessions.note: Full schedule is detailed in the comments section,

syllabus:
Biological systems are made of mixtures of heterogeneous cell populations that are difficult to characterize using conventional bulk methods. Today, a deeper understanding of biological systems requires applying state-of-the-art genomics methods with single-cell resolution. Indeed, single-cell genomics technologies provide a high-resolution and comprehensive view of the transcriptome of the different cellular constituents of tissues, organs, and even whole organisms under different states or conditions, pushing the frontiers in our understanding of normal physiology and disease. In recent years, several platforms for unbiased single-cell analysis have been developed. Amongst them 10x Genomics, the current leading commercial solution for high throughput single-cell RNA-seq analysis, makes this technology available to researchers in the academy, hospitals and industry. Yet, single cell analysis requires proper understanding of its capabilities and limitations.
The course will be composed of a comprehensive introduction to the field, a hands-on session, single cell data analysis, and a single cell genomics interpretation. You will be introduced to single-cell genomics technologies and learn conceptual tools for understanding and designing single-cell based experiments, with an emphasis on single cell gene expression profiling. This will include hands-on practice of the 10x Genomics technology and interpretation of the data generated. Other single-cell genomics tools will also be covered, such as multiomics solutions, including analysis of surface protein expression and gene expression in the same single cell, chromatin accessibility at the single-cell level (single cell ATAC-seq), and CRISPR-based gene perturbation with single-cell resolution. Examples of applications of these technologies will be discussed in a seminar format.
learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course students should:
• Understand the concept of single-cell expression profiling
• Understand the unique features in single cell data analysis
• Get acquainted with the different single cell genomics platforms
• Understand the molecular processes and barcoding usage involved in single cell genomics experiments
• Get acquainted with analytical approaches for single cell analysis
• Design a single cell genomics based experiment relevant for his/her own project
• Interpret single cell data results in current publications

title: Spatial Omics: Exploring Cutting-Edge Technologies
syllabus:
Biological systems are composed of complex heterogeneous cell populations. During tissue disruption, to obtain biological data, spatial information is lost. Advances in tissue level/spatial technologies, such as spatial transcriptomics, multiplexed immunofluorescence, mass- spectrometry-based metabolite and protein imaging, and other imaging-based spatial technologies, enable biologists to study single-cell gene and protein expression and metabolite occurrence yet retain spatial context. This provides valuable information on cell-cell interaction and signaling, which is crucial to answering critical biological questions in various animal models, tissue types, and clinical samples.
The lab course will expose students to various newly emerging spatial technologies. These include advanced imaging technologies, state-of-the-art spatial transcriptomics technologies, and metabolite imaging. We will present the key features of each of these technologies and discuss how they can complement one another. In addition, we will expose the participants to data analysis tools of these technologies and their integration in solving biological questions.
The course will provide a comprehensive background introduction to the technologies, show how different protocols are used, and train participants through hands-on session data analysis.
learning_outcomes: To expose students of biology to a variety of cutting-edge spatial omics technologies available in different core units in Weizmann. At the end of the course, the student shall be able to design a spatial omics experiment on different platforms based on his/her needs and be familiar with the relevant tools to execute it.

title: Statistical analysis of research data using R
fields: Life Sciences (Computational and Systems Biology Track)
syllabus:
This course aims to familiarize students with executing a variety of statistical tests: t-tests, ANOVA and its different variations, multiple linear regression and more. The principle aim of the course is to enable students to understand which analysis is applicable for each type of data, and execute the proper analyses using R. I will also discuss using AI for statistical reasoning and writing code, so the acquired knowledge is easily applicable for Python as well. The main focus will be on usability and application of statistical knowledge in answering research questions, and less on the mathematical background of the statistical methods. No background in programming is needed.
Topics by week:
Introduction to R
Descriptive statistics
Comparing two populations: t-test.
Comparing two populations - non-parametric tests
One-way ANOVA
Multiple comparisons and contrasts
Two-way ANOVA
Experimental design - randomized block, nested, split-plot
Experimental design - repeated measures
Data transformation, power calculations
Linear regression
Correlation + selected topics
learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course students should be able to:
Determine the appropriate statistical analysis for a given experimental setting.
Plan experiments while considering statistical power, sufficient sample size, and avoiding potential statistical "pitfalls".
Execute a variety of common statistical tests (e.g., t-tests, ANOVA and its different variations, multiple linear regression, non-parametric analysis) using R (although the knowledge obtained will be applicable for commercial statistical software as well).
Critically review statistical analyses conducted in published papers.

title: Statistical Methods in Marine Ecology
syllabus:
Statistical Methods in Marine Ecology  (course code20273492)
The course consists of two preliminary meetings and an intensive week at the IUI.
The preliminary meetings (about 5 hours each) will be held in Zoom and will include lectures and computerized practice. These meetings will take place during the two weeks prior to arrival in Eilat (exact date to be determined later). The participation in the preliminary meetings is mandatory.
The week in Eilat will include lectures, computer exercises, fieldwork and data-analyses.  The days are typically long, often extending into the night. Throughout the week the students work in small groups and present their results at the end of each section.
Major topics covered in the course:
A re-examination of key concepts in statistics: p-values, parameters and their estimates, sampling distributions, hypothesis-testing, effect-size, randomization tests.
Issues in experimental design; namely:  Replication, sample size & power-analyses.
How to validate and curate a data-set.
Assumptions of the general-linear model and what to do when the data deviate from them:
- Normality & heterogeneity of variance: generalized-linear-models for binary & count data
- Hierarchical structure in the data: mixed-effects models
How to deal with multiple predictor variables:
- Multiple regression & co-linearity.
- Model-selection (AIC, model-averaging)
learning_outcomes: To get the most biological insight out of your hard-earned data, you need good insight into the statistical analyses with which you will analyze them. Following this rationale, the course will expand on the basics laid in introductory Biostatistics courses, and introduce some of the more advanced analytical tools which are the staple of quantitative ecological research.

title: Stem cells and tissues disease
syllabus:
This seminar will follow adult tissue stem cells and their role in maintaining tissue homeostasis.
Each week we will focus on specific tissues - mainly the gut, lung, and skin, in which adult stem cells are well studied.
Week 1: introduction of the course by Dr. Moshe Biton and assignment of students to recent stem cell - tissue outcome papers, which will be presented by the students.
Week 2-14: Presentation of two students per week, starting from intestinal stem cells discovery to other tissue stem cells and their role in tissue formation, regeneration, and diseases.
learning_outcomes: This course will add more layers to our understanding of tissue maintenance and how the tissue stem cells play a role in homeostasis and different diseases such as inflammation and cancer. This course will deal mostly with adult stem cells.

title: Systems neuroscience reading seminar
fields: Life Sciences (Brain Sciences: Systems, Computational and Cognitive Neuroscience Track)
syllabus: A reading seminar in Systems Neuroscience, focusing on recent interesting papers on mammalian neural circuits that mediate behavior, cognition, and perception. Particular emphasis will be given to papers using Neurophysiology, Optogenetics and Imaging methods in vivo, as well as to theoretical/modeling papers.
learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of the course, the student will be able to:
• Read critically and discuss the current literature in systems neuroscience.
• Demonstrate knowledge of cutting-edge topics in the field.

title: The Hallmarks of Cancer
syllabus:
The Hallmarks of Cancer  (course code20273422)
Cancer is a systems disease characterized by dynamic and adaptive processes rather than a fixed pathological state. Douglas Hanahan and Robert Weinberg conceptualized this complexity through the framework of the “Hallmarks of Cancer”, which describes the key biological capabilities that drive tumor initiation, promotion, and progression.
This course introduces students to the biological and mechanistic foundations of the hallmarks of cancer, integrating molecular biology with systems-level understanding and incorporating multi-omics data (e.g., transcriptomics and metabolomics) to understand tumor behavior.
The course combines foundational lectures with student-led seminars to promote critical thinking, scientific communication, and engagement with current cancer research.
Part I: Core Concepts (Lectures 1–4)
Introduction to Cancer as a Systems Disease
Introduction to the Hallmarks of Cancer framework
Proliferation and Growth Control
Tumor Progression and the Microenvironment
Advanced Hallmarks and Emerging Concepts
Part II: Student Seminars (Lectures 5–12)
Each student selects a research article from a provided list
Presentation duration: ~35 minutes + 10 minutes discussion
Students are expected to:
* Present background and rationale
* Explain experimental design and methods
* Interpret results (including omics data if relevant)
* Critically evaluate strengths and limitations
learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course students should be able to:
1. Describe the “Hallmarks of Cancer” and explain how it captures the complexity of tumor biology.
2. Critically analyze research articles in cancer biology.
3. Evaluate experimental design, methodology, and data interpretation in published studies.

title: The immune system of bacteria: CRISPR and beyond
syllabus:
The most abundant viruses on earth are phages, viruses that infect bacteria. There are more phages on Earth than stars in the universe, and it is estimated that every second, billions of bacteria on Earth are being infected by a phage. To cope with such frequent phage infections, bacteria have evolved a sophisticated and multi-faceted immune system. An important part of the bacterial immune system is the CRISPR-Cas system, an adaptive immune system that allows bacteria to memorize past infections by storing genetic information “stolen” from the phage in the bacterial genome.
In the past few years, there has been a revolution in our understanding of the bacterial immune system. It has been discovered that in addition to CRISPR-Cas, bacteria encode over 200 different defense systems that allow them to actively defend against infection. Surprisingly, it was discovered that important components of the human innate immune system have evolved from bacterial systems whose role is to protect from phage infection.
The purpose of this course it to gain knowledge on principles of bacterial immunity against viruses, and to expose students to contemporary research in this rapidly developing field. The topics that will be covered are
• How viruses infect bacteria: phage structure, phage life cycle, phage assembly
• The bacterial adaptive immune system: CRISPR - discovery and mode of action
• CRISPR - evolution, applications and diagnostics
• The innate immune system of bacteria: Restriction modifications and additional systems
• Principles of bacterial innate immunity
• The revolution in the discovery of new bacterial defense systems
• Evolutionary origin of human innate immunity in bacterial defense systems
• Regulated cell death in bacterial immunity
• Phages fight back – how phages overcome bacterial defenses
• Phage lysogeny and communication between phages
• Application of bacterial immune systems and of phages in medicine and biotechnology
This short course will be taught in 3 lessons, each lesson of 3 hours.
learning_outcomes: The purpose of this course it to gain knowledge on principles of bacterial immunity against viruses, and to expose students to contemporary research in this rapidly developing field.

title: The interaction between the immune system and the environment: seminars in immunology
syllabus:
The interaction between the immune system and the environment: seminars in immunology  (course code20273462)
Course Syllabus 2026
Part 1: The immune system interaction with the fat in adipose tissue in in health and disease.
•
Introduction to the course. The concept of immunometabolism. Adipose tissue immune cells in health and disease.
•
Adipocyte derived lipid laden exosomes leads to immune modulation
•
T regulatory cells (Tregs) in adipose tissue in leanness and obesity.
•
Sympathetic neuron-associated macrophages regulate adipose tissue thermogenesis.
•
Adipose immune cells remodeling in weight gain and weight loss.
Part 2: The immune system interaction with the microbiota in the gut in health and disease.
•
First study on activation of Th17 cells by Segmented filamentous bacteria (SFB).
•
Interaction of Treg cells with the microbiome.
•
Microbial metabolites: short chain fatty acids modulating gut immune cells.
•
Microbial metabolites: bile acids metabolites control immune cells response.
•
Guest talk  Host-microbiota interactions in health and disease.
•
Interaction of immune cells with the microbiota by IgA production.
•
Guest talk Diet impact on immune cells and the environment interaction.
•
Gut microbiota, diet, immune cells.
•
Final talk and concluding remarks. Immune cells, gut microbiome and metabolic disease.
How does the immune system tolerate the trillions of microbes living in our gut? How does our diet influence immune cell function, and why can excessive food intake lead to chronic inflammation and metabolic disease?
In this course, students will explore these questions and gain knowledge through research studies in the field that focus on how immune cells interact with the environment. These studies will cover various aspects, such as how the immune system responds to an excessive intake of food, leading to obesity and metabolic diseases. The students will also be introduced to the concept of immunometabolism.
Another important topic to explore is the interaction between the gut microbiome and the host, and how this interaction affects both health and diseases. Lastly, the students will be taught about the immune system's ability to sense the environment and the different mechanisms that underlie this sensing process.
Students will gain an understanding of current concepts and recent advances in immunology, metabolism, and microbiome research.
learning_outcomes:
The students will gain knowledge through research studies in the field that focus on how immune cells interact with the environment. These studies will cover various aspects, such as how the immune system responds to an excessive intake of food, leading to obesity and metabolic diseases. The students will also be introduced to the concept of immunometabolism.
Another important topic to explore is the interaction between the gut microbiome and the host, and how this interaction affects both health and diseases.
Lastly, the students will be taught about the immune system's ability to sense the environment and the different mechanisms that underlie this sensing process.

title: Time and rhythms in aquatic systems
syllabus:
Time and rhythms in aquatic systems  (course code20273381)
A 10-day course. The course includes lectures, research projects, guided tours, and seminars. The course consists of two parts. The first part is theoretical, during which students are exposed to a variety of lectures in the field and it ends with an exam. In the second part, the research projects are carried-out and the student seminars are presented.
The course introduces the concept of time and rhythm oscillations in behavior and activity of marine biological systems. For this purpose, the following questions are examined: how organisms measure time, what the biological clock affects physiologically and behaviorally, how the biological clock is structured at the molecular biochemical level, and what environmental signals synchronize the biological clock and periodicity. Special emphasis is placed on biological clocks in relation to the complexity of living environments, from the level of symbiotic relationships to the ecological niche. The students are acquainted with the marine system in the Gulf of Eilat and carry out research projects. The purpose of the projects is to implement the concepts and theories that the students acquire in the lectures on the phenomena that are under the control of the biological clock, in various marine systems such as the tidal environment, horizontal and vertical artificial structures and the coral reef.
The grade structure
Group research project 60%. The report will be submitted about a month after the end of the course.
The discussion on the project results will be written personally, submitted separately by each student and its weight will be 30% of the final grade in the course.
Participation and contribution to the course 10%
learning_outcomes:
Key topics covered in the course:
• Time - what is a unit of time in biological systems, what is periodicity?
• The external clock facing the internal clock
• Adjusting the internal clock to various environmental variables such as light, temperature and lunar cycles in marine environments.
• Biological clocks in marine ecological niches.
• Symbiosis and the biological clock.
• Molecular biochemical structure of the biological clock.
• Evolution of the biological clock.
• The biological clock and metabolic processes.
• Reproduction cycles, the effect of endogenous and exogenous variables.
• Animal sensing, magnetism and gravitation.
• Pineal gland: Melatonin, daily and annual cycles.
• The biological clock under interference.
• Biological clocks in marine mammals.
How social interaction initializes the biological clock in ecosystems

title: Trace Elements in Biology: From biochemistry to cellular Mechanisms and physiology
syllabus:
Trace elements (zinc, copper, manganese, molybdenum, chromium, cobalt etc.) are central to life. While each element is found in tiny amounts in cells, all together they bind to approximately a quarter of all proteins (!!) and are also found in many other biomolecules.
The course is aimed at giving students a structured, discussion-driven survey of how trace elements shape life, from basic chemistry to cellular regulation, organismal physiology, disease and ecosystems. We will open with introductory lectures, covering the history of the field, basic bioinorganic chemistry principles, key discoveries and experimental approaches. For the rest of the semester,  we will delve each week into the basic biology of one or two trace elements, through student seminars. Following that, we will discuss in class  related disease, industrial and ecological implications and highlight the current hot topics/knowledge gaps. Grading will be based on attendance, seminars and a short final assignment.
Lesson 1-4 Introduction to trace elements biochemistry
These will be frontal lectures, covering the field's history and central concepts in bio-inorganic chemistry from the atomic to the cellular level, with emphasis on trace elements biochemistry.
•Biochemical characteristics of trace elements (Lewis acids and bases, soft vs. hard shells, redox state and element speciation. Focusing on atomic characteristics of the d-block elements and halogens).
•Binding affinity of trace elements to amino acid residues and binding geometries within proteins (coordination chemistry, crystal and ligand field theories).
•The Irving-Williams series, “free” vs. “labile” populations of ions in the cell and mis-metalation of proteins.
•Experimental and computational methods in the field.
•Examples of key biochemical reactions supported by trace elements and how they were discovered.
•How pre-historic changes in the earth crust and atmosphere shaped the evolution of trace elements as cofactors in different organisms and pathways.
•What biochemical “tricks” do cells and organisms employ to overcome low bioavailability of essential trace elements and avoid toxicity of heavy metals.
•Competition of heavy metals (such as Cd and Pb) with “biological” metals and their mechanism of toxicity.
Lessons 5-11 Transition metals-focused modules (such as cobalt, manganese, molybdenum, etc.)
In these lessons, we will focus each week on one major element or a small group of related elements. Students will be asked to prepare a presentation that covers the following aspects for each element:
•Key biological pathways at the cellular and organismal level.
•Transporters, chaperones and homeostatic pathways.
•Representative disease mechanisms and model organisms.
Following the presentations, we will have a discussion about how key discoveries were made (highlighting experimental strategies), disease and ecosystems, identifying current knowledge gaps, and what are the hurdles that we need to overcome to fill these gaps.
Lesson 12 - Biology of the halogen-type trace elements (I, Se, F)
Lesson 13 - Synthesis and outlook
Summary lesson where we will revisit key concepts in trace elements biology and discuss recent developments in the field, shifting from element-focused biochemistry to metallomics approaches. At the end of this lesson, the students will get a short final assignment where they will be asked to suggest a holistic approach for studying a current knowledge gap.
learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course students should be able to:
• Explain the basic chemical principles that govern trace element behavior in biological systems (coordination chemistry, redox states, HSAB ligand affinity, etc.).
• Describe the major cellular and organismal pathways that regulate and manipulate trace elements.
• Describe central biochemical reactions and cellular processes mediated by trace elements.
• Explain the physiological role of trace elements in bacteria, yeast, plants and mammalian.
• Identify open questions and knowledge gaps in trace element biology and current experimental approaches.

title: Underwater Colorimetry
syllabus: Colorimetry is the science of measuring color. Color is a subjective sensation defined relative to an observer’s visual system (e.g., the human visual system or a camera) and commonly defined for viewing conditions in clear air. This course—the first of its kind in the world—takes the science of color measurement underwater. Through theoretical concepts, computer simulations, and hands-on engineering, we will explore light and quantitative aspects of color, including underwater color image formation, analysis, visualizing color spaces and comparing colors. At the end of this course, students will be able to properly use trichromatic cameras to capture colors underwater (or, in air) in an objective and repeatable manner, select the right color space to perform analyses, and compare colors captured by different systems in a meaningful way which they can then publish as scientific data. This course is a great introduction to underwater computer vision.
learning_outcomes:
Key topics covered in the course
1. Color producing mechanisms
2. Color perception
3. Color capture (spectrometers, RGB, multi-, hyper-spectral cameras)
4. Image formation in air
5. Digital camera image processing pipeline (i.e., RAW vs. JPG, photofinishing)
6. The CIE (commission internationale de l'eclairage or International Commission on Illumination) system: Colorimetry, Wright-Guild experiments, Standard Observers, CIE XYZ system, RGB system, standard illuminants, CIE chromaticity diagram, color spaces, color difference metrics
7. Image formation underwater
8. Underwater colorimetry

title: Being in the body: taking a break and finding inspiration through movement improvisation
fields: Obligatory instruction courses or enrichment courses
syllabus:
Being in the body: taking a break and finding inspiration through movement improvisation  (course code20278071)
Course objectives:
* Creating a conversation between direct lived experience and the life sciences and thinking about life.
* Developing somatic (body-mind) awareness and movement skills through mindful movement improvisation.
* Developing a personal practice of being in the body and somatic pleasuring.
Sensations and feelings precede language and symbols and they tell us important things with precision. This is our instinctive intelligence and it can also be cultivated consciously.
* Using the somatic methods as soft skills applied to the students specific scientific work.
* Creating community and developing skills of being and learning together playfully.
Course structure:
13 weekly classes of 120 min in the dance studio.
Experiential/movement time roughly 80 min. Lecture/discussion roughly 40 min.
We will also play with overlapping them - talking science while moving.
Class 1: Opening circle, introduction, sharing expectations, wishes and questions. Basic tools: feeling at home in the body and studio, attending to breath, body scanning,  following what feels good – ‘somatic pleasuring’, attending to gravity. Moving/being together. Exteroception, proprioception and interoception.
Class 2: Initiation of movement from different places in the body. The body is extended in space, thought is not. Comparing somatic awareness with feelings and thought. Quanta & qualia. The hard problem of consciousness.
Class 3 : Differentiation & integration. Part & whole. Figure & ground. Left and right hemispheres? The process of embodiment. Body-Mind Centering - Experiential anatomy and developmental movement, Movement principles in the field of gravity.
Class 4: What is pleasure? The difference between liking and wanting. Opioids and dopamine. Kinds of pleasure. Para-sympathetic and sympathetic, can we correlate the neuro-science with our experience on the floor in the studio? How does each inform the other?
Class 5: Contact improvisation – principles and techniques of sharing weight. The experiences while dancing contact in the light of opioids, dopamine and also oxytocin.
Class 6: Group improvisation –  Some improvisation scores. From solo to group.
alone together. Seeing and being seen.
Presentation of יחיד יחד
Class 7: Space - The 6 directions, 3 dimensions and 3 planes of movement. The movements in the joints. The skeleton – initiating movement from different bones and joints. FoldUnfold qigong.
Class 8: Space continued - “The ant-man” - Experiential regression through the orders of magnitude from meter to micron and back. What does life feel like at each order of magnitude? Guided imagination/somatisation tour of the cell. Cellular awareness.
Class 9: Measuring. What is our relationship with anything, and with our data.
Class 10: Group improvisation – composition, group improvisation as a simulation and/or exploration of a scientific research question. How to use the group to investigate playfully together a specific student’s research question.
Class 11 :Being in the body improvisation, unknown topic and student presentations
Class 12: Being in the body improvisation, unknown topic and student presentations
Class 13: Being in the body improvisation, unknown topic, student presentations and closing circle.
learning_outcomes:
Improved sense of well being, a sense of community, inspiration, creative ideas and new soft tools
for scientific research.
Learning outcomes:
Students should be able to continue and develop their own practice of being in the body for their wellbeing and as a way to approach their  research more personaly, intuitively and imaginatively.
Students might have a stronger sense of the connectedness between different domains of their life and their scientific work and have greater resilience in coping with its challenges.
Students will hopefully have more interesting questions about everything and a deeper connection with their scientific journey.

title: A reading course on fundamental Concepts of Number Theory
syllabus:
Number theory, nicknamed the "queen of mathematics" by Gauss is a classical and beautiful subject. In this reading course we will taste some of the field's basic notions:
-Basic methods.
-Diophantine equations.
-Approximations of irrational numbers.
-Elliptic curves and modular forms.
-Applications of characters; quadratic reciprocity and Dirichlet theorem.
-Prime number theorem.
-Combinatorial and probabilistic number theory, partitions.
-Algorithmic number theory.
-A bit of P-adic analysis.
-Geometry of numbers.
-A taste from algebraic number theory.
learning_outcomes: The student will acquire some of the basic methods of number theory, and will get to know classical, including non elementary results of the field.

title: A seminar on knots, braids and relations to physics
syllabus:
Knot theory is a beautiful  branch of topology whose basic questions are which types of knots (embeddings of a circle in the 3-space) can be isotoped to the unknot (the standard embedding of the circle as a unit circle in the xy-plane), and how to classify different knots .
Although the questions themselves can be explained to people without mathematical background, the answers and proof techniques tend to be surprisingly sophisticated and are many times related to advanced mathematics and physics.
In this course we shall learn the basic notions of knot theory, and concentrate on knot invariants, which are the main tool for distinguishing between different knots. We will additionally encounter closely related braid group.
We will meet the basic invariants, for example coloring, linking and framing. We will then move to more sophisticated polynomial invariants. We shall then continue to one or more of the following subjects: quantum invariants, Khovanov homology (the categorification of the Jones polynomial), finite type invariants (including Kontsevich's theorem) or the volume conjecture. We will also learn physics perspectives on knots and braids.
learning_outcomes:
1. The student will know the basic notions of knot theory.
2. The student will study several types of knot invariants and their connections with other areas of mathematics and physics.

title: A workshop in problem solving
syllabus:
We will study various methods and techniques in solving mathematical problems (most will require a knowledge of first degree in Math and for the others I'll provide some short reading tasks before hand). We will also prove some classical and some very modern beautiful theorems from different areas of mathematics.
Every week about 10 new problems will be assigned and we will discuss the solutions of the problems from previous weeks.
learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course students should be able to:
• Address unfamiliar problems
• Master techniques and methods for solving problems in various areas of mathematics.
• Learn some classical theorems and their proofs from different areas of mathematics.
• Work on problems as an individual or as part of a team.

title: Active LLM paper reading
syllabus:
This class is an active reading class akin to the esteemed Prof. Raffel's role-playing and the wonderful local version, by Prof. Scwartz. Each week a paper will be read by all participants, each focusing on a different scientific skill related to the paper. The outcomes of the homework would be the basis for discussing the paper and the skills in class. While each of us works earnestly on our parts at home, we will discuss hard topics as a group as needed.
The course will pick 14 papers in contemporary Large Language Models and Artificial Intelligence topics (from core new inventions to foundations).
Moreover, it will focus on learning academic soft skills to accompany the discussions.
Those will be decided after the first meeting and will accommodate student goals, examples include:
Critical paper reading, reimplementation, communicating science, science in the open, writing, (graph) design, and literature review.
Warning: the course is not for the faint of heart. It will include discussions and be open for failure and learning from it, but is meant to be hard work in preparation for each class and is designed to challenge the students and allow them to learn. We will aim to pick papers that are hard and to have little handholding in advance, learning the foundations together with cutting edge topics.
learning_outcomes:
The students will learn about topics in Large Language Models that go deeper than common applications, ideally deeper understanding, and methods. Occasionally, theoretical or philosophical aspects, might appear as well.
Moreover, one can expect to look for academic skills to challenge and hone and to acquire more than the knowledge about the field, also important soft skills.

title: Advanced Algebraic Topology
syllabus: Homotopy groups, Freudental Suspension and stable homotopy groups, long exact sequence of a fibration, Serre spectral sequence, Steenrod operations, computations of low degree homotopy groups of spheres.
learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of the course, students will be able to carry out computations in algebraic topology involving fibrations and spectral sequences, and will understand when and how these techniques can be effectively applied.

title: Algebraic topology
syllabus:
Quotient Spaces, Cell Complexes, simplicial complexes
Homotopy,  Homotopy Equivalence, Deformation Retractions,
Classification of Surfaces
Fundamental Group, Covering Spaces,
Simplicial homology, .Singular homology, Cellular Homology, Relative Homology, long exact sequence of a pair, excision, Mayer–Vietoris, geometric meaning via pseudomanifolds, Brouwer fixed-point theorem, euler characteristic, invariance of dimension, Cohomology, Cup product, Universal coefficient theorem.
Time permitting, we will get through as much of this as we can.
learning_outcomes:
By the end of the course, students have:
•
Conceptual intuition:
•
When you walk down the street and see the same bus twice, you will consider the possibility that you are not in the universal cover.
•
You will be comfortable with the idea of homotopy type, recognizing when spaces are quasi “the same” for topological purposes.
•
You will see and understand cycles, both geometrically and algebraically.
•
Core skills:
•
Compute fundamental groups of standard spaces (spheres, tori, surfaces, CW complexes).
•
Use covering space theory to classify covers and connect them with subgroups of the fundamental group.
•
Calculate homology and cohomology groups of key examples (spheres, projective spaces, surfaces) using tools such as exact sequences, excision, Mayer–Vietoris, and cellular homology.
•
Apply invariants (Euler characteristic, homology, cohomology ring) to distinguish spaces and solve problems.
•
Applications & broader vision:
•
Understand the classification of compact surfaces.
•
Appreciate major results (Brouwer fixed-point theorem, invariance of dimension) as consequences of algebraic topology.
•
Develop geometric insight into abstract algebraic structures, bridging computation and visualization.

title: Algorithms, Games, and Economics
syllabus: In this course, we will explore Algorithmic Game Theory, a field at the intersection of computer science, game theory, and economics. We will study how to design algorithms that perform well even in environments where agents act selfishly. Examples of such environments include auctions, resource allocation problems, and emerging cryptocurrency markets like Bitcoin. Additionally, we will apply algorithmic perspectives to analyze the performance of various economic markets. Toward the end of the course, we might delve into recent research directions, such as using algorithmic lenses to analyze problems from behavioral economics or blockchain economics.
learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course students should be able to:
• Demonstrate familiarity with the basic notions of algorithmic game theory.
• Understand some current important research directions in the field.

title: Basic Topics 1
syllabus:
This course will both review and extend a number of basic mathematical tools which are generally useful in applications and are typically assumed as prerequisites for many of the current courses. The lectures will focus on the following topics:
• Linear Algebra: Jordan forms. Special classes of matrices (unitary, Hermitian, normal, positive definite, stochastic). Singular value decompositions. Pseudoinverses. Linear systems of equations.
• Normed linear spaces: Norms. Basic inequalities. Inner product spaces. Orthogonal systems. Projections, Orthogonal projections, Mean square approximation.
• Differential and difference equations: Systems of first order differential equations. Higher order scalar equations.
• Matrix valued functions: Mean value theorems. Fixed point theorems. The inverse function theorem. The implicit function theorem. Newton's method.
• Optimization: Extremal problems. Lagrange multipliers. Convexity.
• Matrices with nonnegative entries: Perron-Frobenius theorem. Birkhoff-von Neumann theorem. von Neumann's inequality, Ky Fan's inequality.
learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course students should be able to:
• Demonstrate familiarity with the basic tools of linear algebra with special emphasis placed on the ability to compute.
• Calculate Jordan forms.
• Solve systems of linear equations.
• Compute projections (both orthogonal and skew), best mean square approximation and applications of singular value decomposition.
• Apply the acquired knowledge to multivariable calculus (including implicit function theorems and extremal problems with constraints).

title: Cube Complexes
syllabus:
Nonpositively curved cube complexes were introduced by Gromov in his 1987 essay on “hyperbolic groups” which founded the field “geometric group theory”.
While Gromov suggested them as a simple source of higher dimensional ex- amples, nonpositively curved cube complexes have emerged as one of the central objects in the field. A considerable portion of combinatorial group theory owes its soul to hidden nonpositively curved cube complexes. Indeed many ideas related to splittings of groups or combinatorial rewording can be reinterpreted elegantly us- ing cube complexes. Moreover, nonpositively curved cube complexes have become increasingly important in parts of geometric group theory, and provide a natural stage for the study of hyperbolic 3-manifolds, most arithmetic hyperbolic lattices, artin and coxeter groups, small-cancellation groups, the JSJ splitting, codimension- 1 subgroups, median spaces, spaces with walls, and a(T)menability - the “opposite” of Kazhdan’s property (T).
Nonpositively curved cube complexes (and the 1-skeletons of their CAT(0) universal covers) have appeared in other places and in other guises in mathematics, for instance: Robot configuration spaces, Phylogenetic Trees, and as Median Graphs.
We will spend the semester learning about these objects and their essential properties: combinatorial, structural, and metric, and their relations to and context within geometric group theory.
learning_outcomes: The students will learn what nonpositively curved cube complexes are, and how they arise in group theory and geometry/topology, and what to do with them.

title: Differential Geometry
syllabus:

The first part is "Analysis on Manifolds", starting from the definition a differentiable manifold, vectors fields, differential forms, integration, Stokes theorem, de Rham cohomolgy.
The second part is "Riemannian geometry": Riemannian metric, parallel transport, connections, geodesics, curvature.
learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course students will be able to:
• Demonstrate intuition and knowledge of the basic theorems in differential geometry.
• Apply the language and tools of differential geometry in other areas of mathematics and science.
• Work with differential forms.
• Understand the intuition behind curvature (at least in two dimensions) and its effects.
• Appreciate the interplay between analysis and geometry.

title: Enumerative Combinatorics and Commutative Algebra
syllabus:
Part I. Solutions of linear equations in nonnegative integers. Applications are given to the enumeration of integer stochastic matrices (or magic squares), the volume of polytopes, combinatorial reciprocity theorems, and related results.
Part II. Face ring of a simplicial complex -- includes a proof of the Upper Bound Conjecture for Spheres.
learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, the student will be able to read and reproduce proofs that combine commutative algebra (Hilbert series, Cohen?Macaulay rings, systems of parameters) with combinatorics (polytopes, triangulations, simplicial complexes), and apply the course's methods to an independent problem ? for e.g., an enumeration via generating functions, or an f-vector/h-vector computation for a specific complex or polytope class.

title: Finite algebraic structures for Computer Scientists
syllabus:
This course is intended for computer science students who have not taken advanced algebra courses as part of their first degree. The course focuses on the theory of finite structures which are important in applications of algebra to computer science, especially for error-correcting codes. Detailed examples will be investigated.
1.         Basics: Fields, rings, groups, vector spaces and their substructures. Homomorphisms of rings, ideals, quotient rings.
2.         Polynomial rings over fields and their properties. The Chinese remainder Theorem and its corollary for the structure of Z/mZ,
3.         Finite Group theory: Introduction, finite cyclic groups and their properties, the fundamental theorem of finite abelian groups.
4.         Sylow's theorems and applications to examples.
5.         The symmetric groups: their conjugacy classes and structure. Simplicity of the alternating group  for .
6.         Finite Simple groups and the classification theorem – survey.
7.         Introduction to complex characters and representations of finite groups
8.         Finite Field theory: Basic extension theorem, Finite fields, their structure and properties. Existence and uniqueness of finite fields of order q for any prime power q. Detailed examples and arithmetic in finite fields.
9.         Wedderburn's theorem that finite division rings are finite fields.
10.       Factorization of polynomials over finite fields.
11.       Counting irreducible polynomials over finite fields. Finding irreducible polynomials for error-correcting codes over finite fields using the Berlekamp algorithm.
12.       The structure of some classical matrix groups over finite fields, conjugacy classes in finite matrix groups, detailed examples.
13.       Vector spaces over finite fields and error-correcting codes: Bilinear forms and orthogonality in finite dimensional vector spaces over fields of characteristic 2.
14.       The theory of linear codes over finite fields of characteristic 2.
Examples: Hamming codes, using the structure of the field of 16 elements to define the BCH double-error correcting code.
learning_outcomes: Computer science students should acquire a knowledge of finite algebraic structures relevant to their research.

title: Generalized Geometry, an introduction
syllabus:
Generalized geometry is a novel approach to geometric structures pioneered by Hitchin in 2003. Developed further by Gualtieri, Cavalcanti and others, it soon became an active topic catching the interest and bringing together the expertise of geometers and theoretical physicists. For example, generalized complex geometry provides a unifying framework for complex and symplectic structures. In it, we can smoothly pass from a symplectic to a complex structure and have generalized complex manifolds that admit neither complex nor symplectic structures. The theory is supported by Clifford algebras and the theory of spinors, and built on previous developments on Courant algebroids and Dirac structures, which arose as the mathematical formalism for mechanical systems in the presence of both symmetries and constraints.
In this introductory course we will isolate the underlying linear algebra from the actual geometry and draw parallelism between the classical and the generalized setting. In this sense, we will start with some linear algebra that is not usually taught at the undergraduate level, continue with the linear algebra of generalized geometry, recall the basic facts about differential geometry of manifolds (most importantly,  integrability), and finally combine all this knowledge to develop generalized geometry.
We will cover the following topics:
I. Linear algebra
- Linear versions of symplectic, complex and Poisson structures.
- The exterior algebra as a language for linear algebraic structures.
- Spaces of structure and torsors.
- Linear hermitian structures.
II. Generalized linear algebra
- The vector space V+V*: the canonical pairing and its orthogonal transformations.
- Isotropic subspaces and annihilators of forms.
- Linear Dirac and generalized complex structures. The type.
- The underlying role of the Clifford algebra and spinors.
III. Geometry
- Manifolds, bundles and Cartan calculus.
- Almost complex structures and non-degenerate 2-forms.
- Integrability: complex and symplectic structures.
- Poisson structures as symplectic foliations.
IV. Generalized geometry
- The Dorfman bracket and the Courant algebroid TM+T*M. The group of generalized diffeomorphisms.
- Dirac structures: geometric interpretation as foliations, type-change structures, integrability in terms of spinors.
- Generalized complex structures and type change.
- Is there anything between complex and symplectic? Is there anything beyond complex and symplectic?
learning_outcomes:
Upon completion of the course, the students
- will have a good understanding of geometric structures,
- will be able to distinguish its linear-algebraic and geometric features,
- will achieve a working knowledge of concepts such as maximally isotropic subspace, exterior form, spinor, Clifford algebra, Cartan calculus and integrability.
- will acquire a good basis on Dirac and generalized complex geometry.
- will be acquainted with a recent mathematical theory with applications both in mathematics and theoretical physics.
- will be able to independently read relevant literature on the topic.

title: Intersection Theory
syllabus: Chow rings, Grassmannians and Schubert calculus, Chern classes, Grothendieck Riemann-Roch theorem.
learning_outcomes:
Learning Outcomes:
By the end of the course, the student will be able to move fluently between the geometric picture (moduli/parameter spaces, degeneracy loci) and the algebraic computation (Chow ring, Chern classes) underlying a given enumerative problem.
More precisely, they will be able to:
Compute Chow rings of basic varieties (projective space, products of projective spaces) using generators and relations.
State and apply the key formal properties of intersection theory (proper pushforward, pullback, projection formula) to compute intersection numbers.
Translate enumerative geometry problems (e.g., counting lines, conics, or other loci satisfying incidence conditions) into computations in a Chow ring.
Compute the Chow ring of the Grassmannian in terms of Schubert classes, and state Pieri's formula and the Giambelli formula for expressing Schubert classes in terms of special (Chern) classes.
Apply Schubert calculus to solve classical enumerative problems (e.g., the 2,875 lines on a quintic threefold-style counts, or simpler line/plane incidence problems) by multiplying Schubert classes.
Define Chern classes of vector bundles axiomatically (via the Whitney sum formula, normalization, and functoriality) and via Schubert calculus on Grassmannians (as the classes of degeneracy loci), and compute Chern classes of standard bundles (line bundles, tangent bundles of projective space, tautological/quotient bundles on Grassmannians).
Use Chern classes and the formula for the Chern class of a tensor/dual/quotient bundle to compute characteristic classes appearing in enumerative problems (e.g., via excess intersection or degeneracy loci).
State the Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch theorem for vector bundles on smooth projective varieties, and the Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch theorem for a proper morphism, including the roles of the Todd class and Chern character.
Compute the Chern character and Todd class of a vector bundle or variety in examples (curves, projective space, projective bundles).
Apply Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch to compute pushforwards of Chern classes/Chern characters along a morphism (e.g., a projective bundle or blow-up) and recover classical formulas (e.g., for the Chow ring of a projective bundle, or genus/degree relations on curves).

title: Introduction to Computational Imaging
syllabus:
Computational imaging (CI) is a discipline at the intersection of computer vision, image processing, optics, and AI. Its goal is to expand the capabilities of conventional imaging by combining novel imaging techniques with advanced algorithms. Modern computational imaging techniques power every smartphone camera—from stunning portraits to low-light photography —they are, in fact, what make smartphone cameras work.  Computational imaging research, however, strives to go beyond the capabilities of conventional imaging altogether, yielding "cameras" that can capture videos at the speed of light, see around corners or below the skin, and capture speech and music directly from the vibrations they create on object surfaces.
This course lays the foundations of computational imaging while also covering some state-of-the-art research. Tentative topics include:
• The modern image processing pipelines, basic optics, the image formation model (lenses, aberrations, sensor noise, and imaging in color), and computational light transport.
• Advanced image and video editing algorithms like filtering, gradient-domain processing, and deconvolution.
• Advanced image acquisition techniques like light-field imaging, coded photography, focal stacks, depth from defocus, time-of-flight imaging, 3D scanning, and more.
This course involves hands-on experience through multiple homework assignments, in which you will implement various foundational computational imaging algorithms covered in class. The final project consists of creating a short 5-minute (CVPR-style) video describing a recent hot CI paper.
learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of the course, the student will gain an understanding of the fundamentals of modern imaging, advanced imaging techniques, and advanced computational imaging algorithms.

title: Introduction to the theory of algebraic D-modules
syllabus:
1. Algebraic properties of modules over the Weyl algebra D=Dn.

filtrations.
(ii) Noetherian properties.
(iii) Associated varieties, Hilbert polynomials. Dimension and degree of a D-
module.
(iv) Basic inequality.
(v) Holonomic D-modules and their properties.

and right D-modules.
(ii) Digression on the theory of generalized functions and distributions.
(iii) Regularization of distributions xs and Qs using differerential equations.

(iii) Direct image functor

6. Further applications to analysis: regularization of di
fferent type of integrals.

7. D-modules on smooth affine algebraic varieties.

If time permits:

title: Introduction to Verification
syllabus:
Program testing can be used to show the presence of bugs, but never to show their absence!  - Edsger W. Dijkstra, 1970
Beware of bugs in the above code; I have only proved it correct, not tried it.  - Donald E. Knuth, 1977
As the world increasingly depends on software, e.g., to control our finances, drive our cars, and manage our medical devices, how can we tell whether that software will be correct, secure, or reliable? Testing for such properties is theoretically impossible, and notoriously difficult and ineffective in practice. Software verification can, in principle, provide such guarantees with the certainty of a mathematical proof. While verification has historically been difficult to apply at the scale of realistic software systems, a series of recent advances suggests we may be at an inflection point, as various research groups have successfully proven rigorous properties about critical software components, including OS kernels, compilers, and distributed systems.
The course will provide a broad introduction into the field of formal methods and verification. We will introduce the key ideas of this active research field: its motivation, the chief problems it aims to solve, and the main algorithmic techniques and ideas that have been developed to tackle these problems. We will also become familiar with some practical formal verification tools, including SAT solvers, SMT solvers, and program verifiers.
A tentative list of topics to be covered: SAT Solving - DPLL and CDCL; SMT Solving - DPLL(T) and Nelson-Oppen; Hoare Logic; Weakest Precondition Calculus; Abstract Interpretation; Model Checking, Interpolation, and IC3/PDR; Recent advances in verification of distributed systems and in application of large language models in verification.
The final grade will be composed of 50% homework assignments, and 50% final project. The homework assignments are individual, and the final project can be completed in teams of two students. The course includes 2 hours of lecture per week but counts as 3 credit points as the homework and final project will require significant dedication.
The course draws inspiration from the following courses:
• UC Berkeley's EECS 219C: Formal Methods: Specification, Verification, and Synthesis
• Stanford's CS 357: Advanced Topics in Formal Methods
• CMU's 15-811: Verifying Complex Systems
• UT Austin's CS389L: Automated Logical Reasoning
learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course students should be able to:
• Describe basic concepts, principles and algorithms in the field of formal methods and verification.
• Critically read recent research papers in verification.
• Apply the acquired knowledge in their own research.

title: Mathematics of machine learning and machine learning for mathematics
syllabus:
The success of machine learning is evident from its achievements but far from being mathematically understood. This course combines a purely mathematical approach to some aspects of machine learning with an account of the major achievements of machine learning in mathematics.
The mathematical foundations of machine learning date back to the middle of the twentieth century. We will take a purely mathematical approach, without entering in statistical learning theory, to introduce and discuss the basic concepts and ideas.
On the other hand, the effective use of machine learning for mathematics is very recent. Since the 2021 Nature article ‘Advancing mathematics by guiding human intuition with AI’, many applications have  followed. We will learn the basic mathematical notions needed to understand them, explore their algorithms and discuss the nature of their results.
Finally, the students, in small groups, will tinker with the code of an approach of their choice and share their experience through a presentation. For the most advanced and interested students, there will be the opportunity to deal with a new project in collaboration with the lecturer.
Additionally, we expect to have a few invited lecturers to tell us more in depth about some aspects.
We will cover the following topics:
I. What machine learning does from a mathematical viewpoint.
• How to approximate a function? The class of neural networks, loss functions, gradient descent and back propagation.
• What to approximate functions for? Supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning [SB+98].
• Why can we approximate functions? A formal proof [LLPS93].
• What is really happening? Interpretability and Shapley values [Sha53].
Expressivity and the importance of depth.
• Other approaches: Kolmogorov-Arnold networks [LWV+25].
II. Applications
• Knot theory: relating knot invariants [DVB+21], unknotting [ABD+24].
• Graph theory: counterexamples via reinforcement learning [Wag21].
• Linear algebra: matrix multiplication algorithms [FBH+22, KM25].
• Geometry: predicting dimensions in algebraic geometry [CKV23], the Hirsch Conjecture [SWW+25].
• Combinatorics: the cap set problem through FunSearch [RPBN+24], extremal combinatorics with PatternBoost [CEWW24].
• Number theory: generating conjectures with the Ramanujan machine [RGM+21].
• Representation theory: Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials [DVB+21].
• Dynamical systems: global Lyapunov systems via symbolic transformers [ACH24].
III. DIY
• The students will register their interest in a topic, level of expertise and mention other students they would like to work with.
• Depending on their answers, they will be distributed into small teams to work on the code of one of the applications.
• Each team will share their findings in a 30-45 min presentation.
• The most motivated and skilled teams will be offered an additional research question.
Some excellent online resources are: [MLW22, MCA23, Gri24].
learning_outcomes:
Upon completion of this course, the students:
• will have a solid mathematical understanding of the main concepts of machine learning.
• will have familiarity with several applications of machine learning in various areas of mathematics and a deeper understanding of one of them.
• will be able to apply machine learning techniques in mathematical research problems.

title: Proofs from The Book
syllabus:
The seminar will consist of students giving a lecture of between 45 and 90 minutes. The lectures will cover gems in mathematics and computer science that have particularly elegant and concise proofs. The lectures count towards 70% of the final grade. Attendance counts for 10%.
At the end of the course each student will be examined in my office according to the following procedure: I will announce at the end of the course ten selected theorems among those  that we encountered. If the student is not happy with the note they chose they may request to choose another note, with a second topic, in which case they commit to present the second topic. title: Quantum Cryptography
syllabus: This course studies the foundations of cryptography in the presence of quantum information and quantum computation. The emphasis is on formal security definitions, computational assumptions, reductions, and proof techniques specific to quantum adversaries and quantum cryptographic objects. Topics may include quantum money, tokenized signatures, one-shot and other unclonable cryptographic primitives, pseudorandom quantum states and unitaries, the quantum random-oracle model and compressed-oracle techniques, proofs of quantumness, classical verification and delegation of quantum computation, quantum homomorphic encryption, and quantum key distribution. The precise selection of topics will depend on time, student background, and current research developments.
learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students should be able to formulate and analyze cryptographic security definitions involving quantum states, quantum algorithms, quantum auxiliary information, and quantum oracle access; explain how quantum information can serve as cryptographic resources; understand representative results in the field; adapt reductions, hybrid arguments, and indistinguishability proofs to the quantum setting; use standard quantum-information tools such as trace distance, fidelity, purification, and partial trace in cryptographic arguments; and read and critically evaluate research papers in theoretical quantum cryptography.

title: Randomized Algorithms
syllabus: Algorithms that are randomized, i.e. use coin tosses during their execution, are central in many computational scenarios, and have become a key tool in Theoretical Computer Science and in application areas. The course will cover the development and use of such probabilistic techniques, including some of the following topics: Concentration results; Simulating randomness, in particular limited independence; Load balancing; Routing algorithms; Randomized rounding; Sampling and sublinear algorithms; Algorithms in the data stream model; Communication protocols and the sketching model.
learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course students should be able to:
• Analyze probabilistic events and randomized processes.
• Design algorithms that use randomness, and analyze their performance.
• Make use of basic tools such as first and second moment, concentration bounds, balls and bins, birthday paradox.
• Describe and apply algorithmic paradigms that rely on randomness like hashing, sampling, sketching, and streaming.

title: Reinforcement Learning
syllabus:
Course Description: The combination of deep learning (DL) with reinforcement learning (RL),
known as deep reinforcement learning (DRL), is one of the most exciting fields of artificial
intelligence. It has led to agents with superhuman skills in games such as Atari and Go, progress in
robotic control, and more recently important developments in offline RL, imitation learning, RLHF,
and reasoning models. This course is an introduction to reinforcement learning and deep
reinforcement learning. The first part covers classical RL foundations, while the second part
introduces deep RL methods and selected recent advances.
Course Objectives:. Theoretical and algorithmic understanding of reinforcement and deep
reinforcement learning. Practical understanding of the presented algorithms through implementation
in programming exercises.
learning_outcomes: Formulate sequential decision-making problems as Markov decision processes (MDPs). Understand the principles and algorithms underlying modern reinforcement learning. Implement and evaluate fundamental reinforcement learning algorithms. Design and analyze reinforcement learning solutions for practical problems. Critically assess and apply reinforcement learning methods in research and real-world applications.

title: Representations and Characters of Finite groups
syllabus:
The theory of the representations and characters of finite groups is central both to algebra and group theory. The tools that the theory develops enable us to reach a deeper understanding of the structure of a finite group. We shall study classical ordinary, or complex, representations and characters, and then develop briefly the main theorems and ideas of modular representations and characters. Modular representation theory deals with representations of finite groups over a field of prime characteristic, and their connections and relations with the ordinary representations. The resulting beautiful theory which was developed by Brauer, gives additional insights into the structure of the group.
Group algebras, Maschke's theorem, structure of finite-dimensional semi-simple algebras over a field, centre of the group algebra. Ordinary (complex) irreducible representations and characters of finite groups, character tables, orthogonality relations. Central characters and algebraic integers. Burnside's theorem. Induced characters, Frobenius reciprocity. Modular representations of finite groups.Brauer characters, blocks and decomposition numbers. Defect groups, the Brauer correspondence, Brauer's first main theorem. Blocks of cyclic defect and Brauer trees, Dade's theorem.
learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of the course students will be able to:
• Demonstrate proficiency in calculating the ordinary and modular characters of finite groups.
• Comprehend the connections and relations between the ordinary and modular character theory of a finite group.
• Apply the theorems and methods of character theory to obtain insights, understanding and deep theorems in the structure of finite groups

title: Topics in Machine Learning Theory
syllabus:
This course will provide a self-contained introduction to the theory of machine learning and some of its currently-researched areas. It will be roughly divided into two parts: (1) Statistical learning theory; and (2) Theory of deep learning.
Important disclaimer: The course is theoretical in nature, aimed at students with a strong math/theoretical CS background, and focuses on theorems and proofs rather than machine learning applications.
learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course students should be able to:
• Describe basic concepts, principles and algorithms in the field of machine learning theory.
• Apply their acquired knowledge in their own areas of research.

title: Topics in statistical inference and learning
syllabus:
The course will cover several classical as well as modern topics in statistical inference, including:
- Statistical Modeling, parametric vs. non-parametric models
- The Maximum Likelihood Principle
- Non-parametric models, Kernel Density Estimation, Curse of Dimensionality
- High Dimensional statistics
- Sparsity
- Low rank models
- Spectral Methods
learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course students will be familiar with several classical and modern topics in statistics, the involved challenges, techniques to address them and their theoretical foundations.

title: Navigating Academia: Science, Identity, and Practical Tools for First-Generation Student
fields: Obligatory instruction courses or enrichment courses
syllabus:
Navigating Academia: Science, Identity, and Practical Tools for First-Generation Student  (course code20278012)
Instructor: Dr. Meytal Eran-Jona (sociologist, gender expert, Head of Diversity and Inclusion Office at WIS). The course will also host scientists from the Weizmann Institute and experts in communication skill.
Credits: 1 credit
Course meetings: Bi-weekly, 1.5 hours each
Institution: Weizmann Institute of Science
Course Purpose
The course aims to equip Master’s students, particularly those who are first-generation in higher education or come from underrepresented backgrounds, with conceptual, analytical, and practical tools for understanding and navigating the academic environment.
It integrates critical theoretical perspectives on science, culture, identity, and power with practical skill-building in scientific communication, writing, and interpersonal relations, supporting graduate students’ academic success.
Target Population
The course is intended for Master’s students across all faculties (except Science Teaching) who:
• identify as first-generation in higher education (neither parent attended university), or
• come from socially peripheral or minority backgrounds.
Course Schedule (Overview)
• Introduction: Identity, belonging, and “the Hidden Curriculum”
• Structures of power and inequality in Higher Education
• Science as a diverse field: Culture, Intercultural communication, and scientific practice
• Scientific presentations: principles and practice
• Scientific Writing: writing an academic paper
• Conflict management in the lab/ research group
• Final integration session
Course Assignments & Evaluation
To support reflective learning and integration of theory with practice, evaluation is based on three components:
1. Short Reflective Assignment - 30%
2. Final Integrative Assignment – 50%
3. Attendance – 20%
Active engagement and class participation in a discussion-based learning environment.
learning_outcomes:
By the end of the course, students will be able to:
Theoretical Understanding
• Analyze the academic environment using key sociological concepts such as cultural capital, habitus, intersectionality, imposter syndrome, and the hidden curriculum.
• Develop a reflexive understanding of how identity, culture, and social structures shape scientific knowledge and academic trajectories.
• Critically examine power relations and inequalities within academy.
Applied Skills
• Apply effective strategies for scientific writing, presentation, and communication.
• Use analytical and interpersonal tools to navigate mentoring relationships, cross cultural environments, and academic conflict.
Articulate personal academic experiences through conceptual lenses, strengthening agency and self-efficacy.

title: AMOS Seminar
syllabus:
The Atomic, Molecular, and Optical Science (AMOS) seminar is a mix of lectures by Weizmann AMO students, scientists, and invited guests.
Student talks may focus on any scientific topic that interests them – from journal club-style presentations to discussions of their own research, or anything in between. In-depth discussion following each talk is an integral part of the seminar. Students who give a talk during the year will receive 1 credit point.
Presenting at the AMOS seminar is an expected part of the PhD program in AMO. MSc students and postdocs are also encouraged to volunteer.
learning_outcomes: Student speakers will gain experience presenting scientific topics to a scientific audience. The AMOS seminar also provides an opportunity to receive feedback on a topic that interests them.

syllabus:

title: Intensity Interferometry and the HBT effect
syllabus: This course introduces the principles and applications of intensity interferometry, from the foundational Hanbury Brown–Twiss experiment to modern implementations in optical astronomy and astrophysics. Topics include photon statistics, coherence theory, second-order correlations, stellar angular diameter measurements, atmospheric and instrumental considerations, detector technologies, signal processing, and future large-baseline intensity interferometer concepts. The course emphasizes both theoretical foundations and practical instrument design.
learning_outcomes:
• Explain the principles of stellar intensity interferometry and the Hanbury Brown–Twiss effect, including photon statistics and second-order coherence.
• Apply coherence theory and the Van Cittert–Zernike theorem to relate intensity correlations to astronomical source properties.
• Analyze the sensitivity, limitations, and performance of intensity interferometers.
• Understand the design principles of intensity interferometry systems, including telescopes, detectors, timing electronics, and correlation methods.
• Compare intensity and amplitude interferometry and evaluate their roles in modern astronomical instrumentation.
• Interpret results from existing and emerging intensity interferometry experiments.
• Apply concepts from quantum optics and signal processing to astronomical measurements.
• Critically evaluate current research and propose new concepts in intensity interferometry and related technologies.

title: Nuclear Physics - Structure and Reactions In Lab and Astrophysics
syllabus:

title: Quantum computing hardware
syllabus:
This course surveys the leading physical platforms for quantum computing, with an emphasis on how physics constrains and enables hardware design. We begin with an overview of the quantum computing landscape: key metrics, error sources, and the requirements imposed by fault-tolerant architectures.
We then dedicate lectures to major platforms: superconducting qubits, trapped ions, neutral atoms, photonic quantum computing, and solid-state spin defects. Each platform is presented by an expert in the field. The course concludes with a discussion of scalability, error correction overhead, and the prospects for fault-tolerant quantum computation across platforms.
learning_outcomes: Students will gain a broad understanding of the main physical platforms for quantum computing, their operating principles, key figures of merit, current experimental state of the art, and future directions. Students will develop the ability to critically evaluate hardware trade-offs and connect physical implementations to quantum error correction requirements.

title: Shotgun Seminar
syllabus:
The seminar will cover a wide range of advanced and fundamental topics in astrophysics. In each lecture, we will cover one chapter in a book or paper. All students are expected to read the chapter and be ready to give the lecture, while in each lecture, one student will be randomly selected to give the lecture.
Among the topics are: radiation transfer & radiative processes, compact objects, galactic dynamics, microlensing, and more.
Journal Club - please use the past year text.

The talk will preferably be on their own research work. However, the main focus would be on the presentation structure and appearance, content, timing, and speech. The course will start with an introductory lecture and continue with a series of lectures from the participating students, followed by discussions.
learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course students should be able to:
• Present seminars in a coherent way for different audiences
• Demonstrate proficiency in stressing the main points of the work, independently of the length of the talk.
• Form good communication with the audience
• Address questions related to the topic of the presentation

syllabus:

Upon successful completion of this course students will be able to qualitatively and quantitatively address the mechanical state of modern materials using the intrinsic approach, identify geometric frustration and predict how it will affect the mechanical state of a body. The student will be proficient in differential geometry as it arises in uses in mechanics, and be able to digest contemporary research papers, lectures and seminars in soft condensed matter, biological physics and related fields.
This course includes equal amounts of mechanics and differential geometry. It is particularly recommended to anyone who seeks to learn the tools of differential geometry in a physics oriented setting.

title: Communication, Collaboration and Learning Across Professional Boundaries
syllabus:
Mathematics and science education are constituted by multiple professional communities (e.g., teachers, disciplinary experts, researchers, teacher educators), each operating within distinct discourses, practices, and professional jurisdictions. Furthermore, each of these communities is itself highly diverse - teachers may base learning on problem solving, investigation, or practicing procedures, and researchers may rely on fundamentally different theories of learning and of teaching that often make use of the same words (knowledge, learning, development, understanding) in crucially different ways. In spite, or perhaps in light of this diversity, cross-community collaboration is prevalent in almost every aspect of science education: research, teacher preparation and professional development, curriculum development, etc. While such diversity is often treated in these contexts as a source of fragmentation, recent research reconceptualizes these differences as boundary phenomena that can serve as resources for learning, innovation, and institutional change.
This course examines learning across professional boundaries and jurisdictions through a discursive and interactional lens. Building on contemporary research on boundary crossing, dialogical learning, and research–practice partnerships, we focus on how differences in epistemology, professional obligations, and evaluative frameworks shape communication and collaboration across communities. Particular attention is given to structured forms of cross-community dialogue (e.g., video-based inquiry, co-design partnerships, task-based collaboration) and to the conditions under which such interactions may be productive is various senses, such as leading to consensus or supporting learning across boundaries.
Drawing on cases of cross-community interaction in various contexts (e.g., research-practice partnerships, teacher preperation or professional develpoment, theory networking), students will analyze how professional boundaries and jurisdictions are negotiated, when they constrain learning, and when they become generative sites for innovation.
The course is designed for graduate students in mathematics and science education and its curriculum will be finalized in light of participating students’ profile and interests.
learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course students should be able to:
• Conceptualize professional boundaries: Analyze differences in discourse, norms, and obligations across communities as boundary phenomena rather than deficits.
• Analyze cross-community interaction: Identify and distinguish different forms of productiveness in professional dialogue.
• Examine professional jurisdictions: Explain how instructional decisions are shaped by situated disciplinary and institutional obligations rather than fixed norms.
• Use analytical frameworks on empirical cases: Apply concepts such as boundary objects, professional obligations, reflection mechanisms, and dialogical learning to real cases.
• Design for cross-boundary learning: Propose how to structure and facilitate cross-community interaction in specific research or practice contexts in ways that support productive collaboration.
